articles.title: Tech Moguls Worth Combined $2.2 Trillion Attending Trump-Xi Dinner: See Who’s Going
articles.summary: Dire warnings about AI risks set the backdrop for the dinner, where many of the world’s wealthiest and most influential will gather.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is slated to host Chinese President Xi Jinping at a state dinner this week, where they'll be joined by billionaire tech moguls collectively worth trillions of dollars amid a backdrop of warnings about AI potentially threatening human civilization.

Trump and Xi will meet on Thursday and likely discuss AI, trade and tariffs as the U.S. and China have maintained tariffs against each other despite agreements that reduced the levies last year.

The White House will then hold a state dinner that evening featuring both presidents and several billionaire leaders of the world's most valuable tech companies, several of whom are among the wealthiest people in the world.

Elon Musk , whose estimated net worth of $962.5 billion makes him the wealthiest person in the world by a massive magnitude, will reportedly attend.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos , whose $374.3 billion fortune ranks as the largest behind Musk's, will be at the dinner, as will world's fourth-wealthiest person: Michael Dell ($271.5 billion).

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg ($252.5 billion) will attend the dinner alongside Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ($198.1 billion) and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella ($1.4 billion), according to Bloomberg , which noted Apple executive chairman and ex-CEO Tim Cook ($3.1 billion) will attend as well.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ($3.3 billion) and president Greg Brockman ($25.5 billion) will be at the dinner, CNBC and Bloomberg reported, as will Google CEO Sundar Pichai ($1.6 billion).

It is unclear if Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei ($15.5 billion), who urged top AI firms to slow down their model development, will be in attendance for the dinner, though he is slated to brief the United Nations Security Council alongside Altman on Wednesday, according to ABC News. Altman and Musk swiftly joined Amodei's calls earlier this month for slowing the pace of frontier AI development.

Thursday's dinner will be hosted after a senior researcher at Anthropic warned of a more than 10% chance AI could "kill all humans" within the next decade, provoking Amodei's call for a slowdown.

Over $2.2 trillion. That is the cumulative net worth of the tech moguls who will attend or are expected to attend the White House state dinner Thursday. Musk accounts for more than 40% of that sum.

WHAT OTHER BUSINESS LEADERS WILL ATTEND THE STATE DINNER?

Qualcomm chief Cristiano Amon is planning to attend, according to Bloomberg, as is Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, Politico reported.

Jacob Coxon, who resigned as an Anthropic researcher early this month and previously worked for OpenAI, said in a tweet some AI companies were "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." Coxon warned of "superhuman systems that can hack anything" but noted he was optimistic for AI companies to coordinate on safety. Days later, Amodei called for a slowdown on AI development, with both Altman and Musk echoing his warning to "pace the frontier." Amodei identified some risks including the loss of control over infrastructure, cyberattacks, bioterrorism, economic disruption and takeover of the internet by autonomous AI agents. Trump, meanwhile, has doubled down on his support for AI development and said his administration will not "hinder or stifle" the AI industry despite warnings from experts. Trump has pushed for AI growth to continue at top speed, framing it as a race the U.S. must win against China.

articles.title: Stung by Trump, machinists union campaigns for affordability in midterms
articles.summary: One of the largest labor unions in the US targets eight battleground states in ‘workers v billionaires’ campaign
articles.body:
The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM), one of the largest labor unions in the US, has launched a "workers v billionaires" political campaign tour targeting members in eight battleground states and encouraging them to support pro-worker candidates in the midterms.

IAM has nearly 700,000 active and retired members in North America, covering workers at corporations that include Boeing, Lockheed Martin, United Airlines and Harley-Davidson. The union is targeting members and voters in Maine, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Arizona, Nevada and Illinois.

"We made a strategic commitment that we're going to be the most engaged that we have ever been in the history of our union in working," said Brian Bryant, international president of IAM. "We're living in an economy that only favors billionaires and does not favor working people, and it's time that Congress and this administration realize who they should be looking out for."

Bryant emphasized that several union members , including those with IAM, voted for Trump in 2024 because of promises that he would fix the economy and make things more affordable. Throughout his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump repeatedly claimed : "When I win, I will immediately bring prices down, starting on day one."

Yet since Trump took office, inflation has increased from 3.0% in January 2025 to 3.4% in August 2026, health insurance costs are soaring due to the expiration of Affordable Care Act subsidies and gas prices are on average $1 a gallon higher due to Trump's war with Iran.

The union will "send a message to this administration that what the status quo is right now is not acceptable, and they're going to have to stand up and pay attention to working people", Bryant said.

Jason Gayler, president of IAM local 776A in Fort Worth, Texas, said his state "is more purple than what people put out to be". As Democrats are seeking to flip several seats, polls are showing that races are the most competitive they've been in decades.

"The price of just the cost of living in north Texas now has absolutely skyrocketed, and it's starting to really affect a lot of our members, which is motivating them to back candidates that focus primarily on the working class," Gayler said.

He also noted that the machinists recently elected their first rank-and-file member to the Texas senate; Taylor Rehmet, president of the IAM's Texas state council, won a special election in January, flipping a state senate district that Trump won in 2024 by 17%.

Shay Blodgett, an Alaska Airlines worker in Phoenix who is helping to lead IAM's political program in Arizona, said the union has worked to oppose Republican-led state legislation that would have restricted public sector workers' ability to organize and supported the Arizona AFL-CIO "labor 2026 blitz" campaign .

"We've been conducting member-to-member engagement this summer, reaching out, asking members what matters to them," Blodgett said. "We heard them loud and clear. The No 1 thing was the economy, cost of living, fuel prices, healthcare and food costs."

Co-workers have expressed regret over voting for Republicans in the last election, especially since transportation workers are exempt from the temporary no-tax-on-overtime deduction that was passed as part of Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill Act that was passed last summer.

"The majority of our airline workers in the state will be entering contract negotiations in early 2027, and we need elected officials that will fix the economy and allow airline workers to fulfill the American dream of home ownership and raising families in Arizona," Blodgett said.

Rich Howell, former president of IAM local 1776, a longtime member of the union and worker at Philadelphia international airport, said the union is supporting Democrats in Pennsylvania who are trying to flip four congressional districts and the state senate while maintaining control of the governorship and statehouse.

Trump "said he was going to bring down the prices a year and a half ago. That was his campaign message. If you go back and see all the promises, there wasn't one that he held," Howell said.

He noted this is a difficult election year due to the amount of money billionaires are pouring into politics – more than $1.6bn in the 2026 midterm elections so far – but noted that "money doesn't buy a race".

"Trump put the tariffs on, cutting more jobs, hurting more people in our industry," Howell added. "It's billionaires versus the workers, and that's the stance we're making. They are getting rich and we're paying for it. We're paying for it out of our pockets."

• This article was amended on 23 September 2026 to clarify that more than $1.6bn has been poured into the 2026 midterm elections so far. An earlier version incorrectly stated it was $1.6tn.

articles.title: ‘National security’ is Trump’s catchall excuse as he tries to turn DC into a fortress
articles.summary: The Trump administration is leaning into national security arguments to remake parts of Washington in line with the president’s fancy and creating a buffer.
articles.body:
A version of this story appeared in CNN's What Matters newsletter. To get it in your inbox, sign up for free here .

The Trump administration is leaning into national security arguments to remake parts of Washington in line with the president's fancy and to create a buffer around him.

Either the administration is legitimately worried about armed invasion, nervous about an attack at a time when the president has started one war and ordered the kidnapping of another country's president, or it's looking for justifications to spend taxpayer money on President Donald Trump's pet projects.

The concept of national security is a catchall for presidential power. Trump has tried to use it to justify tariffs; deportations; extrajudicial attacks on alleged drug-trafficking boats; and his expansionist designs on Greenland, among many other things.

Now, national security is turning the capital into fortress DC.

First, the East Wing demolition was rebranded from ballroom preparation to massive underground military installation. Security needs were meant to justify the approximately $400 million in taxpayer dollars requested for the project despite Trump's previous promise it would be privately funded.

Troops will be in the streets for the rest of his term

The deployment of National Guard troops who mill around tourist areas has been extended through the end of Trump's term , which will cost another $1.4 billion, according to one estimate the Pentagon provided to lawmakers. That's on top of the hundreds of millions the move has already cost.

The triumphal arch will feature snipers and drones

Now the triumphal arch Trump wants erected will do double duty as a sniper's nest, weapons cache and drone port, according to the president's social media post.

The press corps is now a national security threat

The Justice Department is defending the president's decision to expel reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House by arguing in court that stories about his ballroom project and the Iran war could amount to a national security risk . A court hearing is expected Wednesday.

There's already a buffer around Trump and his White House

The executive mansion is one of the most secure locations on Earth, and it has had a fallout shelter and command center since the 1940s.

Presidents have long invoked national security to justify their actions and to expand their powers, in large part because the courts are reluctant to stand in their way on that subject.

And conservative Supreme Court justices bought in to the idea that a new East Wing must be built immediately for security reasons. A historically minded citizen has no cause to sue, they reasoned, in part because of the threat of attack.

"The Secretary of the Army, for example, represents that '[t]he height and mass' of the planned above-ground ballroom are 'crucial' to shield the planned underground military installation 'from kinetic impacts,' and that, without such height and mass, 'engineers would need to dig impractically deep.'"

Chief Justice John Roberts joined the court's liberals in arguing the construction was likely unlawful. Without mentioning national security, he noted that Congress has not authorized the construction or authorized appropriations to pay for it, as required by law.

Fences to the north. Fences to the south

In addition to the military complex under the East Wing, the buffer around the building has grown, at least for the moment. The Ellipse to the south of the building has been closed since the UFC match over the summer , apparently to regrow grass destroyed at the event and also to construct a helipad . Down the street from the Ellipse, a large portion of the National Mall has also been closed until 2027 for turf and tree repair, according to the National Park Service .

Lafayette Square to the north of the building has been fenced off for fountain repair. But the Secret Service has kept the area closed as it proposes plans to permanently install fencing around the park, which free speech advocates argue should be maintained as a place for gathering and protest.

The park would reopen, according to Secret Service plans presented to the Commission on Fine Arts and the National Capital Planning Commission , but gates would make it easier to close again. Most recently, the Secret Service said the Ellipse and Lafayette Square should remain closed through the end of the month during a visit by Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

A sniper's nest between a cemetery and a river

Rebranding the triumphal arch as a national security priority is the strangest riff on Trump's frequent citation of national security to get things he wants.

Never mind that the site planned for the arch sits in the middle of a traffic circle in the middle of a highway between the Potomac River and Arlington National Cemetery with ample military sites, including the Pentagon and Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall, nearby.

When plans were presented to the National Capital Planning Commission, which has been stuffed with Trump supporters, there were descriptions of public spaces rather than a military site. Apparently, the plans are changing, at least according to Trump's social media post.

Trump on Sunday described the arch as "a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage."

That sounds like the kind of defensive capability needed to repel an attack rather than to maintain law and order.

CNN's chief law enforcement and intelligence analyst, John Miller, noted that US law precludes the use of the military against US citizens, so who exactly are these snipers protecting the city against?

The DC police, the FBI and multiple other agencies have SWAT teams in the city, he said, which makes the need for a triumphal arch full of military gear confusing.

"It's not much of a Trojan horse in that the cat's out of the bag," Miller told CNN's Pamela Brown on Monday. "Anybody who would target Washington, who was a foreign adversary, would know what it was, what was in it, and where to hit."

The arch would be 250 feet high, still safe for air traffic going into nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the Federal Aviation Administration, which recently gave approval for the arch , although its green light said nothing about military drones or snipers.

Let's all hope the US is never at the point where military snipers are taking aim across the river from the top of a triumphal arch.

The administration has prioritized national security spending; Trump has promised a "Golden Dome" missile defense shield to protect the US from a potential missile attack. It is modeled on Israel's Iron Dome, although the difference in scale between the US and Israel is making things difficult and the cost astronomical.

That defense shield is one reason Trump also wants to drastically increase military spending, ramping up to about $1.5 trillion, an increase of about 40%, although Congress has not yet approved the jump.

The British sacked the city in 1814. Al Qaeda terrorists hijacked commercial planes and flew one into the Pentagon in 2001. But the size and geography of the US make any type of siege against the city unthinkable. It was heavily fortified and encircled by military forts during the Civil War, when it was a main target of the Confederate army. President Abraham Lincoln even came under fire during a visit to Fort Stevens in the northern part of the city. Some of those forts have been turned into parks today.

The former estate of Confederate general Robert E. Lee, directly across the Potomac, which had been seized by the Union during the war, was bought by Congress and converted into Arlington National Cemetery, outside of which Trump wants to install the arch/sniper/drone complex.

Trump and some of his supporters have described the influx of immigrants to the US as an invasion, but there's no evidence to suggest DC is in danger of attack. The question over whether the administration can use the wartime Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to deport suspected gang members without a court hearing has been left unresolved as the people in question were ultimately deported under different authority.

But dangers faced by presidents frequently come from within

Trump has been the subject of assassination attempts, and in 2020, during his first term, he was rushed into the White House bunker during tense protests in Lafayette Square.

The fact of those threats is helping Trump to use the necessity of national security to get what he wants now, even if he didn't make the argument until planning for his ballroom and arch were well underway.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

articles.title: Trump is giving China's Xi a warm welcome. But criticism is loud on Capitol Hill
articles.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington is getting a much chillier reception on Capitol Hill than at the White House as lawmakers from both partie...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington is getting a much chillier reception on Capitol Hill than at the White House as lawmakers from both parties use the visit to denounce China's actions on the world stage.

Lawmakers have long found little downside to taking a hawkish tone on China, but the U.S.'s war with Iran has inflamed tensions as U.S. officials accuse China of propping up Iran's economy and supplying its military with components and intelligence, endangering U.S. service members in the Middle East.

In speeches, letters, press conferences and hearings, lawmakers from both parties aired criticism of Xi's visit. Their actions and events stand in stark contrast to the warm welcome that Trump gave Xi on Wednesday as he arrived in Washington for a lavish state visit.

Sen. Roger Wicker, the chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, took to the Senate floor Tuesday night, offering a list of issues for Trump to raise with Xi, but not before suggesting that Xi shouldn't have been asked to visit Washington at all.

"Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party," Wicker said.

Wicker seemed particularly taken aback by the honor of a state dinner. Over the salad course, Wicker said the president could ask Xi about the Chinese Navy's harassment of Filipino fishermen and sailors. Then, while the servers are "switching from chardonnay to cabernet at the fancy state dinner," perhaps the president could turn to the issue of Taiwan , he said.

He went on to say he hopes some progress will be made when the president discussed trade and artificial intelligence with Xi. But concluded with this: "During every minute of dialogue, our commander in chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America."

House committee weighs in with a critical video

Ahead of Xi's visit, the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party released a highly critical video that had been viewed more than 245,000 times on X. In the video, the committee details Xi's rise to power starting in 1974 and ends by labeling him "the biggest opponent of freedom and liberty in the world."

The House created the panel in 2023. It's held several hearings on human rights issues in China and advocates for legislation on an array of economic and military issues. For example, the committee's chairman, Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., recently introduced a bill that would prohibit the manufacture or sale of Chinese cars in the U.S.

Republican senators press for Taiwan aid

Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and three other Republican senators used the Xi visit to press the Trump administration to move ahead with aid and arms sales to Taiwan.

In a letter, they reminded Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he had previously stated that "deterring an invasion of Taiwan must be our top priority." And they noted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had once declared that the U.S. "will not let our allies and partners be subordinated and intimidated."

China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales , most prominently during a summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a "very good negotiating chip" with China.

"It is difficult to imagine how the United States might credibly project influence deterrence in the Indo-Pacific," the senators wrote, "if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities."

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and three other Democratic senators held a press conference to warn against the U.S. weakening export controls for advanced semiconductor chips and equipment. They're concerned that such exports could erase the U.S.'s lead in artificial intelligence over China.

They touched on voter concerns about the safety of artificial intelligence and contrasted Democrats' call for greater regulation with the president's call to "encourage it, not rein it in."

"We must reject the false choice Trump keeps making," Schumer told reporters. "We can and must both maintain our lead on AI by restricting China's access to our technology and put up guardrails to mitigate AI's risk."

Meanwhile, on the Senate floor, Democratic senators urged Trump to confront Xi directly about the support his country is providing Iran.

"If we want to bring this war to an end, we need to cut off the outside support that allows Iran to keep fighting, and that starts with China," said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democratic lawmaker on the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title: Senado: candidatos apresentam propostas para desenvolvimento econômico | G1
articles.standfirst: Postulantes participaram de série de entrevistas exibidas pelo NE1 nesta quinta-feira (24).
articles.summary: Postulantes participaram de série de entrevistas exibidas pelo NE1 nesta quinta-feira (24).
articles.body:
Candidatos ao Senado em 2026 falam sobre propostas para o desenvolvimento econômico — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Os pernambucanos vão eleger, no dia 4 de outubro, dois novos senadores para representar o estado no Congresso Nacional. Dando continuidade à série especial iniciada no fim de agosto, o NE1 apresenta, nesta quinta-feira (24), propostas e opiniões dos candidatos nas eleições 2026.

Nesta quinta semana da série, o tema escolhido foi "Como atuar no Senado para melhorar o ambiente de negócios e ampliar as oportunidades de desenvolvimento econômico no estado". Foram entrevistados os candidatos com mais de 5% das intenções de voto na pesquisa Quaest divulgada na quarta-feira (23) .

Cada candidato teve 40 segundos de fala. Humberto Costa ( PT ) foi convidado, mas, por incompatibilidade na agenda, não compareceu.

Confira os candidatos ao Senado, na ordem de veiculação dos vídeos:

"A nova Reforma Tributária vai acabar com o ICMS, que é um imposto do estado, e no lugar dele vai existir o Fundo Nacional de Desenvolvimento Regional. E no Senado, a gente vai ter a condição de garantir que a parcela que Pernambuco vai receber desse fundo seja justa e suficiente para que a gente continue se desenvolvendo, para que a gente gere emprego, gere renda, infraestrutura para trazer novas empresas e oportunidades. Lá no Senado, eu vou brigar muito para que a gente não fique atrás de nenhum estado, do Sul, do Sudeste, de nenhuma outra região do Brasil. E que Pernambuco possa voltar a ser protagonista. Eu tenho condições de estar lá brigando, lutando, para que isso aconteça".

"Como Senador da República, eu vou buscar o equilíbrio nas contas públicas para que a gente possa reduzir a taxa de juros, que está muito elevada, sacrificando empresas e trabalhadores, reduzindo o poder de compra da classe trabalhadora brasileira e afetando diretamente as empresas. Ao mesmo tempo, também defenderei a redução da carga de impostos, que é muito elevada, principalmente para a micro e pequena empresa. Por fim, buscar financiamento que possa incentivar a pequena e média empresa no estado de Pernambuco para que elas possam gerar mais renda e oportunidade de trabalho para todo o estado de Pernambuco".

"No Senado, vou trabalhar ao lado da governadora Raquel Lyra para fortalecer o setor produtivo do estado de Pernambuco. Para que a gente possa lutar para diminuir a taxa de juros. O Brasil não aguenta mais os juros deste tamanho. Quem pega um empréstimo, muitas vezes não consegue pagar pelas altas taxas de juros. E nós temos que fortalecer o setor produtivo, aumentando o crédito e diminuindo os impostos. Votei a favor da Reforma Tributária e vou lutar para que essa reforma seja implementada, diminuindo o imposto daquele que produz no estado de Pernambuco".

articles.title: Thor Dantas disputa governo com foco em habitação e infraestrutura | G1
articles.standfirst: Médico infectologista, professor universitário e ex-gestor de saúde lidera a coligação 'Frente Ampla pelo Acre'. Candidato aponta 'apagão de obras' e propõe planejamento técnico para gerar emprego e renda.
articles.summary: Médico infectologista, professor universitário e ex-gestor de saúde lidera a coligação 'Frente Ampla pelo Acre'. Candidato aponta 'apagão de obras' e propõe planejamento técnico.
articles.body:
O médico infectologista e hepatologista Thor Dantas é o candidato do Partido Socialista Brasileiro (PSB) ao Governo do Acre nas eleições deste ano pela primeira vez. Liderando a coligação 'Frente Ampla pelo Acre', o candidato apresenta um plano de governo estruturado em torno do planejamento técnico e da retomada de obras de infraestrutura.

Formado em Medicina pela Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), doutor pela Universidade de Brasília (UnB) e professor associado da Universidade Federal do Acre (Ufac), Thor acumula quase três décadas de atuação na rede pública de saúde.

No serviço público, ele já atuou como diretor do Pronto-Socorro de Rio Branco , presidente da Fundação Hospitalar do Acre (Fundhacre) e secretário-adjunto estadual de Saúde. Após disputar uma vaga na Câmara dos Deputados em 2022, o médico agora pleiteia o Executivo Estadual.

A principal bandeira defendida por Thor Dantas nesta campanha é a reestruturação da capacidade de investimento do Estado em obras de engenharia e infraestrutura, área que o candidato aponta estar defasada nos últimos anos.

Para o candidato, o investimento em obras públicas é o caminho mais rápido para impulsionar a economia local, gerar novos postos de trabalho e melhorar as condições sociais da população, tanto na capital quanto no interior.

"A gente está discutindo aqui uma das maiores necessidades do Estado do Acre no momento. O Acre vive um verdadeiro apagão de obras públicas nos últimos oito anos. O Acre enfrenta graves problemas de infraestrutura para poder dar o seu desenvolvimento econômico, experimentar o desenvolvimento econômico que a população precisa", avaliou o candidato.

Thor Dantas (PSB) concorre ao governo do Acre pela primeira vez — Foto: Reprodução/Rede Amazônica

Construção de estradas, ramais e habitação popular

Dentro do planejamento de infraestrutura, Thor propõe a recuperação de estradas estaduais, a manutenção constante de ramais, essenciais para o escoamento da produção agrícola, e a criação de programas de moradia popular.

Além do foco em infraestrutura urbana e rural, o plano de governo do candidato do PSB prevê o fortalecimento dos serviços públicos essenciais, como saúde e educação, integrados a um modelo de gestão eficiente para otimizar os recursos do estado nos próximos quatro anos.

"Discutir aqui obras públicas, engenharia, infraestrutura com quem sabe, com quem faz, é fundamental. O nosso plano prevê uma retomada da capacidade do Estado de investir em infraestrutura, da capacidade do Estado de planejar e de executar obras públicas, de construção de estradas, de ramais, de casas populares. O Acre precisa voltar a investir naquilo que mais gera emprego, naquilo que mais gera renda e naquilo que traz retorno social imediato", completou.

Thor Dantas (PSB) tem como foco a infraestrutura caso seja eleito governador do Acre — Foto: Reprodução/Rede Amazônica

A Rede Amazônica definiu uma série de entrevistas ao vivo com os candidatos mais bem colocados na primeira pesquisa Quaest contratada e divulgada pela emissora. Além de estar entre os cinco primeiros, o candidato precisava atingir pelo menos 5% das intenções de voto na pesquisa estimulada.

As entrevistas na TV ocorreram entre os dias 14 a 17 de setembro, durante o Jornal do Acre 1ª Edição. Cada candidato teve 25 minutos para responder às perguntas, incluindo as considerações finais.

Segunda-feira (14): Tião Bocalom (PL) - não compareceu

Quarta-feira (16): Alan Rick (Republicanos) - confira o balanço completo

Quinta-feira (17): Mailza Assis (PP) - confira o balanço completo

Candidatos ao governo do Acre nas eleições de 2026 — Foto: Reprodução

Os demais candidatos que não ficaram entre os primeiros colocados ou não atingiram 5% das intenções de voto na pesquisa tiveram espaço em reportagens gravadas de dois minutos.

articles.title: Empresa que movimentou recursos de filme sobre Bolsonaro recebeu dinheiro do crime organizado, diz ministro da Fazenda | G1
articles.standfirst: Dario Durigan fez a avaliação após a terceira fase da Operação Carbono Oculto nesta quinta-feira (24), que contou com a participação da Receita Federal.
articles.summary: Dario Durigan fez a avaliação após a terceira fase da Operação Carbono Oculto nesta quinta-feira (24), que contou com a participação da Receita Federal.
articles.body:
O ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, afirmou nesta quinta-feira (24) que a "Entre Investimentos", que segundo as investigações da Polícia Federal (PF) foi usada para intermediar repasses ao filme sobre o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, recebeu dinherio do crime organizado.

"Nós estamos falando de uma administradora, de um grupo empresarial, que é o Grupo Entre, que recebia dinheiro tanto do Master quanto do crime organizado e dentro de um mesmo bolso. E esse recurso foi utilizado para ocultar patrimônio, para lavar dinheiro, para corromper", disse Durigan.

O ministro deu a declaração após a terceira fase da Operação Carbono Oculto, da PF, que revelou ligação entre a máfia dos combustíveis e o esquema de precatórios do Master.

Entre os alvos das buscas da operação desta quinta estão Humberto Arthur Tupinambá Neto, ex-executivo do Banco Genial, seus irmãos, André e Bruno Tupinambá, além do empresário Antonio Carlos Freixo Junior, conhecido como “Mineiro”, dono da Entre Investimentos.

A Entre Investimentos faz parte do grupo Entrepay foi liquidada em março deste ano pelo Banco Central (BC).

A decisão do BC à época foi motivada pelo “comprometimento da situação econômico-financeira” da Entrepay, além de irregularidades no cumprimento das normas que regem o setor e prejuízos considerados capazes de expor credores a um risco anormal.

"Tudo indica que o recurso que dá liquidez para essas operações [Dark Horse] vem de uma mesma entidade, vem de um mesmo bolso. Aí é muito complicado você identificar o que que é cada coisa. Se tem dinheiro do PCC, se tem dinheiro de usina do crime organizado, de distribuidora de combustível do crime organizado no mesmo bolso, no mesmo fundo. É um trabalho identificar o que saiu desse fundo, seja para as delações que estejam sendo feitas aqui em Brasília, seja para apurações do Supremo e de São Paulo (...) Mas tudo indica que sim", declarou o ministro.

O empresário afirmou em sua delação — assinada com a PGR em 8 de agosto — que era responsável por "gerar" dinheiro vivo para a equipe de Vorcaro . O dinheiro era entregue em malas e, segundo ele, seria usado para pagamentos de propina.

Mineiro disse ainda que fez sete repasses, a título de "subscrições de cotas", para o fundo Havengate nos Estados Unidos . As transações foram feitas de janeiro a setembro de 2025 e totalizaram US$ 12,333 milhões. Pela cotação de setembro de 2025, esse valor equivalia a R$ 62,8 milhões.

articles.title: Sen. Tim Scott says GOP in "fight for our lives," sees path to holding Senate
articles.summary: With just under six weeks until the midterms, Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina laid out the NRSC's strategy to try to hold onto the Senate amid a tough polit...
articles.body:
In a closed-door meeting with lawmakers, the chair of the Senate GOP's campaign arm made the case that the party can still outrun a difficult political environment and hold on to the Senate in the November midterms, multiple people in the room confirmed to CBS News.

"We're in the fight for our lives with a record number of toss-up races," Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, who chairs the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), told his colleagues during Wednesday's meeting, CBS News has learned.

With just under six weeks until the midterms, Scott said the group will focus its future spending on a handful of tight races where it is either defending GOP-held seats or attempting to flip Democratic seats, the people said.

Scott pointed to Maine, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska as among the seats the party is defending. As for opportunities to go on offense, he named New Hampshire and Michigan.

Semafor was first to report on Scott's comments.

The meeting came as Republicans aim to defend their narrow majorities in the House and Senate — and prepare to face down political headwinds wrought by President Trump's sagging approval ratings, tied in part to voter dissatisfaction with the cost of living and frustrations with the Iran war. Democrats have sought to capitalize on the political environment, mounting strong challenges against GOP Senate candidates in red states like Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Alaska.

Historically, the party that controls the White House almost always loses ground in the midterms. During his closed-door presentation, Scott argued Republicans could follow a trajectory similar to the one their opponents traced in 2022, when Democrats gained a Senate seat despite losing the House and struggling with then-President Joe Biden's rough approval ratings.

Senators were also told during the presentation that Republicans are aiming to take advantage of a Supreme Court ruling that struck down limits on the amount of money groups like the NRSC can spend in coordination with candidates, according to a source in the room.

With a 53-47 majority, the Senate Republican conference can afford to lose as many as three seats and still hold on to the chamber, with Vice President JD Vance serving as a tiebreaker.

One of the most vulnerable GOP-held seats is in Maine, where Sen. Susan Collins is seeking a sixth term in a state that has trended leftward. But Collins — who is running against Democratic former state lawmaker Troy Jackson — has survived tough reelection battles in the past, winning by 8.6 points in 2020 despite being dramatically outspent by her Democratic opponent.

And in North Carolina, a light-red state that Mr. Trump narrowly won three times in a row, Democrats are vying to replace retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis with popular former Gov. Roy Cooper. Most polls show Cooper with an edge over Republican nominee Michael Whatley.

Scott told his Republican colleagues Wednesday that internal polls showed tightening races in North Carolina and Minnesota, where Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is facing off against former sports reporter Michele Tafoya. Minnesota is represented by a retiring Democrat.

A Democrat hasn't won statewide in Texas in over 30 years, but the party's nominee, James Talarico, is running against a polarizing Republican candidate in Attorney General Ken Paxton, who defeated incumbent GOP Sen. John Cornyn in the primary.

Democrats are also looking to flip Senate seats in Iowa and Ohio — two former swing states that have shifted rightward — as well as red-leaning Alaska.

Senate Republicans are aiming to pick up two seats held by retiring Democrats: New Hampshire and Michigan. The GOP nominee in New Hampshire, former Sen. John E. Sununu, comes from a well-known local political dynasty. Michigan Republicans, meanwhile, hope to take advantage of lingering fissures within the Democratic Party after progressive Abdul El-Sayed won the nomination.

Republicans also hope to pick up Georgia's Senate seat, which is held by Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Most polls show Ossoff leading the GOP nominee, Rep. Mike Collins, and Republican sources have previously told CBS News the party is considering whether to scale back its spending on the Georgia Senate race.

articles.title: Major pro-life group threatens to sue Trump FDA over abortion pill's alleged environmental risks
articles.summary: Students for Life of America threatens to sue the Food and Drug Administration, alleging it skipped Endangered Species Act reviews for mifepristone.
articles.body: A leading pro-life organization has formally threatened to sue the Food and Drug Administration, accusing the agency of failing to conduct required environmental testing of the abortion drug mifepristone despite potential risks to the waterways and wildlife. Students for Life of America (SFLA), an anti-abortion advocacy group, filed a notice of intent to sue the FDA on Thursday, hours before Dr. Heidi Overton is scheduled to appear before the Senate for her confirmation hearing to lead the agency. The notice says that after the FDA approved mifepristone in 2000, it never consulted two wildlife protection agencies about the drug's possible harmful effects on federally protected species, which the group argues violated the Endangered Species Act. "We expect these environmental concerns to be taken seriously. I know Dr. Overton is aware of these concerns. Or we expect to see the Trump FDA in court. That's where this will end," SFLA President Kristan Hawkins told Fox News Digital in an interview on Wednesday. PRO-LIFE LEADER SOUNDS ALARM AFTER DOCTOR GETS 6 MONTHS FOR FORCING ABORTION PILLS ON GIRLFRIEND Hawkins said the FDA now has 60 days to respond to SFLA's notice before a lawsuit is filed. Prior to the notice, the group had filed 11 citizen petitions to the agency urging action. In response to one of those petitions on Jan. 15, 2025 — five days before President Donald Trump began his second term — the FDA rejected SFLA's legal argument, saying it was not required to consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service or the National Marine Fisheries Service before approving mifepristone. The SFLA notice cites six studies, four of which did not examine whether mifepristone was present in environmental water samples, to argue the drug may pose environmental risks warranting further federal review. Among the studies cited is a recent paper published in Issues in Law & Medicine, which reported anti-progesterone activity in water samples from three U.S. cities. HAWLEY URGES DOJ PROBE INTO ABORTION PILL MAKER OVER SAFETY CONCERNS Because mifepristone blocks progesterone receptors — preventing the hormone needed to sustain a pregnancy from doing its job — SFLA argues the findings show the drug has made it into the U.S. water supply. "Where do all the babies go in chemical abortions?" Hawkins said. "If we're talking 600,000 to 700,000 abortions a year being induced with chemical abortion pills, where are they happening? She doesn't go to a facility to complete the abortion. The abortion often takes weeks at home. She is told to go and sit on a toilet to flush." The study, however, did not directly detect mifepristone in the water. Instead, it looked for signs of substances that block progesterone, and the researchers said another compound could have produced the same result. Directly confirming the presence of mifepristone would generally require an analytical chemistry technique capable of identifying the substance itself. FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS Hawkins told Fox News Digital that the legal notice against the FDA is not reliant on one study but rather "rests on the failure of the FDA in 2000 to literally follow the law." "This should be something that unites all Americans, regardless of how you feel about the violence of abortion. I certainly am pro-life, I wanna see abortion ended. But we all want clean drinking water," she said. Hawkins said that message has resonated even with students who disagree with her organization's stance on abortion. SFLA has a strong presence on college campuses, with 1,575 active student groups across nearly half of America's traditional four-year universities. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With new leadership at the FDA on the horizon, Hawkins said her organization is reminding the agency of its responsibilities. "Today, Dr. Heidi Overton will be at the U.S. Senate," Hawkins said. "And we want to be very clear that when she gets to her desk, when she get confirmed and she sits down, the first thing she sees on her desk is our notice to intent to sue." "It is high time to hold the abortion industry accountable and to hold our government accountable for upholding our own laws that have been enacted to protect all of us as well as the animals within our country," she added.

articles.title: White House ordered to restore access to banned news outlets
articles.summary: A district court judge ruled the White House violated the Fifth Amendment rights of CNN, MS NOW and Politico by banning them, and granted the plaintiffs a te...
articles.body:
A district court judge ruled that the White House violated the Fifth Amendment rights of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico by banning them, and granted a temporary restraining order for their press access to be reinstated for 14 days.

Outlets that weren't banned but stood in solidarity with their peers suspended video and photo distribution until their peers' access was reinstated, highlighting the importance of press unity in the face of restrictions.

The ruling allows journalists to cover the upcoming meeting between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House, emphasizing the significance of media access in providing visual coverage to the public.

A district court judge ruled the White House violated the Fifth Amendment rights of CNN, MS NOW and Politico by banning them, and granted the plaintiffs a temporary restraining order that forces the White House to immediately reinstate their press access for 14 days.

Why it matters : Had a judge ruled against them, the broader press boycott could've dragged on, leaving the American public without key visual coverage of the White House.

Outlets that weren't banned but stood in solidarity with their peers vowed to suspend video and photo distribution until their peers' access was reinstated.

Zoom in : In a court filing Wednesday, district judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee, said the plaintiffs "have shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim."

"The 'general rule,' is that 'individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them' of a constitutionally protected interest," he noted.

Context : The ruling comes ahead of a meeting at the White House between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, which means journalists will be able to cover the event and the public will get access to video and photography coverage.

Zoom out : The decision marks a huge win for the media, as it reinforces previous precedents set around its Fifth Amendment rights.

In their complaint, the outlets argued the White House violated their First Amendment rights by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoint; and their Fifth Amendment rights for banning them without due process.

Flashback : Judge Kelly oversaw a CNN lawsuit against the White House for blocked access in 2018.

In that case, he granted CNN a temporary restraining order that required The White House restore then-correspondent Jim Acosta's press badge, ruling that the White House violated his Fifth Amendment rights by pulling his credentials without notice or an appeal process.

While outcome of that case isn't binding, it does hold weight in informing Kelly's decision-making. CNN, MS NOW and Politico referenced that case in their lawsuit.

Zoom out : Press freedom lawyers argue the plaintiffs have a strong First Amendment case, given a binding legal precedent set by a higher court.

In 1977, a federal appeals court ruled that The White House could not revoke a journalist's press credentials based on their coverage or viewpoint.

In that case, journalist Robert Sherrill sued the White House for being denied a press pass with no explanation.

That court ruled that once the White House opens up space as a public forum and lets journalists in, it cannot selectively remove access for select reporters based on their viewpoint or coverage under the First Amendment.

What's next: The judge will hear more evidence from the plaintiffs and defendants for the next two weeks, after which time, an appeal is possible.

articles.title: Judge blocks Trump's White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico
articles.summary: The banned news organizations had filed a federal lawsuit accusing the president of violating the First Amendment.
articles.body:
A judge has temporarily blocked President Donald Trump's White House ban on three news organizations, calling it likely unconstitutional and ordering their access be restored.

Trump announced a ban on reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Sept. 18, saying the outlets "constantly write or report fiction or lies" about his administration.

In response, the outlets filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court on Monday, citing their First Amendment rights and demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.

In the complaint , the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House were retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.

The Justice Department's response to the suit argued that the ban did not violate the First Amendment. "Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right," the filing said. The DOJ contends that Trump "has 'compelling interest' in enforcing minimum standards for bona fide journalists and safeguarding national security information."

However, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, blocked the ban for 14 days early on Thursday, describing it as likely unconstitutional and rejecting Trump's contention that it had been put in place on national security grounds.

The president indicated in a Truth Social post on Monday that he would appeal any ruling against him.

Trump's initial ban had prompted four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — to refuse to participate in the White House pool, which is the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events.

As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone typically provided by the pool.

On Monday night, the White House launched a Trump TV YouTube stream. Branded " TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station ," the White House said in its description that it would run videos and highlights of "the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place." The first video showed Trump's remarks on July 3 at Mount Rushmore.

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post , saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press."

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house."

According to CNN , Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban.

On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated.

The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — were listed as plaintiffs in the court filing.

The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement . "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

On Sunday, Trump posted what appeared to be an AI-generated image of trash bags bearing the logos of CNN, MSNBC (MS NOW's former name) and Politico outside the White House.

On Monday, the three news outlets — which are longstanding members of the White House press pool — sued Trump and other members of his administration.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement.

According to the complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House are retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.

"President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint states.

The Washington Post , the New York Times and HuffPost each announced that they would not publish images of Trump's trip to New York on Monday in solidarity with the banned journalists.

Speaking with reporters after arriving at the United Nations on Tuesday, Trump appeared to take issue with the presence of CNN's Kaitlan Collins , saying he was "surprised" to see the journalist.

"You should not be here covering me," Trump said. "You said you weren't going to be covering me."

In a post on X , Collins said she was credentialed by the United Nations to cover the General Assembly.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio also defended the ban in an appearance on NBC's Today show. "We're not closing CNN," Rubio said . "There aren't a bunch of police officers or soldiers kicking down the doors of MSNBC or MS NOW, whatever it's called, and arresting people and unplugging it from the grid. They're just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House."

On Wednesday, dozens of media organizations signed an amicus brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

"The President has indicated that evictions of other news organizations will follow," it states. "The current ban — and any future bans — are intended to impair the critical work of news organizations covering the presidency if this Court does not immediately intervene."

U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected.

During his first term in office, Trump continued the Oval Office's adversarial relationship with the media, referring to the press as "fake news" and the "enemy of the people." It has only escalated in his second.

In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and a federal judge — also Timothy Kelly — ordered Acosta's credentials restored .

A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass .

Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In December, the Pentagon announced new restraints on journalists, who were asked to sign a pledge affirming that they would not gather unauthorized information for publication. News organizations refused to sign the pledge, and temporarily lost their credentials. The New York Times filed suit, and in March, a federal judge ruled that the Pentagon restrictions were unconstitutional. The Pentagon restored press credentials to the journalists who refused to sign the pledge, while imposing a new rule that they can only enter the Pentagon with an escort . The Times again filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed . Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter."
