MS NOW's Akayla Gardner, CNN's Betsy Klein and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett are seen near the White House after all were denied entry on Sept. 19. (AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana)
A view of the White House Briefing Room on Sept. 19. (Graeme Sloan/Getty Images)
A White House staff member reaches for the microphone held by CNN's Jim Acosta as he questions President Donald Trump during a news conference on Nov. 7, 2018. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

articles.title: The unlikely South American ally helping lead Trump's drug cartel crackdown
articles.summary: Ecuador's foreign minister says American forces work alongside Ecuadorian military and police in joint operations targeting drug cartels in Latin America.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Ecuador has emerged as a key regional ally in President Donald Trump’s expanding crackdown on drug cartels and narcoterrorism, with U.S. and Ecuadorian forces working side by side to intercept narcotics shipments and dismantle transnational criminal networks, the country’s foreign minister told Fox News Digital. Foreign Minister Roberto Kury said the increasingly close cooperation with Washington has delivered "a lot of positive results" in recent months, pointing specifically to drug shipments uncovered through U.S. intelligence and joint work on the ground. "There is an intelligence and cooperation from the United States, but there is also always the presence of Ecuadorian military or police. They work together," Kury told Fox News Digital in an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly this week. For Ecuador, the stakes are enormous. Roughly 70% of the world’s cocaine passes through Ecuadorian ports, an FBI official told lawmakers earlier this year, according to the Congressional Research Service, as criminal groups battle for control of trafficking routes carrying cocaine produced in neighboring Colombia and Peru to markets abroad. Meanwhile, Kury noted: "Most of the drugs go to the United States. So that’s why the United States shares the problem." US MILITARY BOARDS, SEARCHES AND SINKS VESSEL ALLEGEDLY SUPPORTING LOS CHONEROS NARCO-TERRORISTS For the U.S., Ecuador has become a proving ground for an early priority laid out in Trump’s foreign policy: using American military power against threats closer to home as Washington turns its attention back toward the Western Hemisphere. The explosion in the drug trade has transformed the small South American country. Once considered one of Latin America’s safer countries, Ecuador is now at the frontline of the region’s cartel fight, fueling a surge in violence that prompted President Daniel Noboa to declare an "internal armed conflict" against criminal groups and deploy the military against them. "We have found many drugs and shipments through this cooperation, so it’s very positive for Ecuador," Kury said of the partnership with the U.S. Asked whether U.S. forces were participating directly in operations against cartels rather than limiting their role to intelligence and training, Kury was unequivocal about the joint nature of the effort, noting, "They work together with our local authorities." But Kury stopped short of giving Washington carte blanche to use military force inside Ecuador when asked whether his government would permit the U.S. to strike a cartel target on Ecuadorian soil. WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES "Ecuador has our sovereignty, and they respect that sovereignty," Kury said, adding that Quito welcomes U.S. involvement "as long as we work together, aligned with our local military and our local police." Kury's comments come as Ecuador has emerged as a testing ground for the Trump administration's effort to take the fight against Latin American drug cartels beyond maritime interdictions and into partnered military operations on land. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has praised Ecuador as the U.S.’s most "aggressive" partner in its Western Hemisphere crackdown. He told reporters during a recent trip to Quito that U.S. and Ecuadorian "elite forces" from both countries "are working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organizations." The expanding partnership comes as Ecuador battles a cocaine trade that President Noboa has estimated at roughly $30 billion a year. The country is looking to Washington for additional help taking on the criminal organizations behind the explosion. Noboa said this week that his government asks the U.S. for help "every day" as Ecuador seeks to choke off a drug trade that has fueled years of violence and transformed the once relatively peaceful South American nation into a key front in the regional fight against organized crime. Kury said Ecuador and other countries in the region need more than funding from Washington as criminal groups increasingly operate across national borders. "Our countries in Latin America have the problem that we need support," Kury said. "We need not only monetary support but also intelligence, technical cooperation." "That’s why we have the Shield of the Americas," he added, pointing to the U.S.-led regional initiative against cartels. "I think that the whole Latin American continent should work together." The growing relationship extends beyond the cartel fight: Ecuador has also agreed to accept some third-country nationals deported from the U.S., part of the Trump administration’s effort to enlist regional partners in carrying out its immigration agenda. Kury told Fox News Digital there are limits and "explicit rules" governing the arrangement, describing Ecuador as a temporary stop rather than the final destination for those sent there. "The deported people come to Ecuador for a few hours, one day, two days, and they are then deported back to their country of origin," Kury said. "So it’s the way to cooperate, and that’s how we support each other, each country." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kury emphasized that Quito wants the expanding relationship with Washington to translate into greater U.S. investment and trade in Ecuador. "The United States is the main trade partner of Ecuador," he said, pointing to opportunities for American investment in mining, oil and gas, energy, tourism and agriculture. "We look not only [for] cooperation in the security side, but we also look to build more jobs in our country, to bring investment from the United States." The U.S. is Ecuador’s largest trading partner, with U.S. exports to the country totaling $7.7 billion in 2024 and accounting for 28% of Ecuador’s imports, according to the Commerce Department. Ecuador uses the U.S. dollar as its currency but does not have a free trade agreement with Washington.

articles.title: Oil prices back up as U.S. and Iran trade threats to expand 7-month war
articles.summary: As Iran responds to Trump's threat of annihilation with its own warning of a possible "new front" in the war, global oil prices are rising again.
articles.body:
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, was trading over $105 a barrel again Thursday as the United Nations General Assembly brought little evidence of progress toward a peace deal. A senior adviser to Iran's supreme leader warned Thursday, after President Trump threatened the Islamic Republic with annihilation , that Iranian forces and their Houthi allies in Yemen could respond to any new U.S. attacks by opening "a new front" in the seven-month war , targeting energy supplies in the Red Sea. A commercial vessel was struck Wednesday in the latest attack in the Strait of Hormuz, killing one crew member and necessitating the evacuation of more than 20 more mariners, according to Oman's navy.

Iran's president says Trump's U.N. remarks forced him to change his own speech

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said President Trump's remarks to the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, about deciding whether to "annihilate" Iran, prompted him to alter his own address to the summit.

"With regard to the statements made by the U.S. president, the text of the speech that had been prepared before the trip for presentation at the UN General Assembly was set aside," Pezeshkian told journalists in New York.

He said it prompted him to change the approach to discussing "ourselves, America's behavior and the actions that Israel is carrying out."

Criticizing Mr. Trump's remarks, in which the U.S. president said he had a "big decision" to make about whether to drive Iran "into hell," Pezeshkian said: "They cannot destroy Iran; Iran is a country that has roots in history."

Referring to Iran's diplomatic activity during the visit, he said meetings had been held with officials from several countries, including the Iraqi prime minister and the Swiss president, with "good understandings and areas for cooperation" discussed.

Through a translator, Pezeshkian told the summit Wednesday that Iran was a victim of Israel and the U.S., and that the U.S. is using the Strait of Hormuz "to impose their aggression upon us."

Iran "will never bow our head or bend at the knee. Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialog and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force," Pezeshkian added.

Iran's IRGC posts video appearing to show cargo ship ablaze after deadly strike in Strait of Hormuz

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps posted a video Thursday on its Telegram social media channel purportedly showing the aftermath of its attack the previous day on a cargo vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.

According to the description provided by the IRGC, the video "confirms that at least one projectile struck the violating vessel on Wednesday morning."

Oman's navy said Wednesday that it had come to the rescue of the vessel's crew, one of whom was killed in the attack on the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao. Oman said 27 crew members were evacuated from the stricken ship.

The strike on a cargo vessel was first reported earlier Wednesday by the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center.

In its social media post Thursday, the IRGC said the ship was targeted for "transiting the Strait of Hormuz along an unauthorized and unsafe route."

Iran has demanded for weeks that all ships wishing to transit the strait seek permission from its military, rejecting repeated U.S. assertions that a southern route through the vital shipping channel, close to Oman's coast, is safe and available.

Oil prices jump as U.N. summit brings no sign of peace deal, Iran and U.S. threaten to expand war

Global oil prices jumped Thursday, with international benchmark Brent crude surging 3% percent to hit $106.24 per barrel before easing slightly as uncertainty swirled around the seven-month U.S. war with Iran.

Hopes for a deal to get Gulf oil and gas flowing freely through the Strait of Hormuz as global leaders gathered for the United Nations General Assembly in New York had sent oil prices down for about two weeks, until Wednesday.

But as world leaders offered little to suggest any progress toward ending the turmoil that has choked tanker traffic in the Middle East, crude oil prices renewed their ascent.

Benchmark U.S. crude rose about 2% to trade just under $94 a barrel early Thursday, while Brent remained up over 2%, selling at over $105 before markets opened in the U.S.

The price for Brent crude has remained much higher than the roughly $72 it cost before the U.S. and Israel jointly launched their war with Iran. Talks between the U.S. and Iran, via mediators, have resumed this week, but nothing concrete has come from the discussions.

The price rises also come as Iran warns that any renewed U.S. attacks — which President Trump has threatened repeatedly to order this week — could draw retaliation with expanded targeting of energy infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea and possibly even the Indian Ocean.

Adviser to Iran's supreme leader warns new U.S. attacks could see expansion of war in Red Sea, Indian Ocean

Major General Yahya Safavi, a senior military adviser to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, warned Thursday that any resumption of hostilities by the United States could see Iran and its allies expand their attacks on global energy supplies in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and possibly even stretch to the Indian Ocean.

"If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait may open before their eyes," warned Safavi, a former commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The Bab el-Mandeb, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, is the Middle East's second major shipping chokepoint, and it has become vital to Saudi energy exports as the ongoing U.S.-Iran war severely impedes traffic in the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz.

"Are they prepared to enter a battle on this front? This is a question they should pay more attention to," Safavi said, asserting that the Houthis had "full control" over the Bab el-Mandeb and access to the Red Sea.

"I think that the connection between the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, will change the battlefield," he said, stressing the link between Iran and its Houthi allies as "a shared destiny — both in terms of common interests and common threats."

"The war front could become broader," he said, extending even "to the Indian Ocean or elsewhere."

Already the Houthis have attacked Saudi ships in the Red Sea and infrastructure and vowed to impose a blockade of the kingdom's Red Sea ports. The group claims it is retaliation for ongoing Saudi military strikes in support of Yemen's government, which has been engaged in a civil war against the Houthis for more than a decade.

8 suicide attempts by U.S. sailors assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln strike group during its record-long deployment, Navy letter says

There were eight suicide attempts by sailors assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group since it began its record-long deployment about 10 months ago, according to a letter from Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao that was obtained Wednesday by CBS News.

CNN was first to report on the letter. A Navy official confirmed it was sent Tuesday.

The deployment of the Lincoln and its approximately 5,000 crew members came under scrutiny after family members of the sailors and members of Congress raised questions last month about the conditions aboard the carrier and concerns about the mental health of its service members.

The Lincoln and its strike group were sent to the Middle East after the Iran war broke out. It has since left the region and is returning to its home base of San Diego.

A defense official told CBS News two of the suicide attempts occurred during active fighting with Iran. The letter covers the entire length of the Lincoln strike group's deployment, which began in November of last year.

The strike group includes the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all the embarked aviation squadrons.

The letter was in response to questions from Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York about reported conditions on the ship. In a statement provided to CBS News, Gillibrand said that what President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members."

That the Trump administration "can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable," she added.

U.S. blockade has redirected 115 commercial vessels, military says

The U.S. military blockade on the Strait of Hormuz has now redirected 115 commercial vessels entering or exiting Iranian ports, according to U.S. Central Command .

The total is an increase of five ships since Monday, when the military last provided an update.

The blockade has become a renewed topic of conflict as Iran and the U.S. renewed negotiations this week at the U.N. General Assembly. Representatives from the United States, including Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, met with Iranian officials on Tuesday and apparently found some common ground, with President Trump saying the meetings went well.

However, on Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei reiterated that no deal will be signed until the U.S. removes the blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.

White House responds to Iranian president's speech at U.N.

President Trump is "courageously" fighting against the Iranian regime, the White House said Tuesday in response to a question about Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's speech at the U.N. General Assembly.

"The Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region," Anna Kelly, White House principal deputy press secretary, said in a statement. "The President is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable."

Through a translator, Pezeshkian said Iran was a victim of Israel and the U.S., and the U.S. is using the Strait of Hormuz "to impose their aggression upon us."

Iran "will never bow our head or bend at the knee. Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialog and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force," Pezeshkian said.

Canada imposes new sanctions on Iran officials, entities

The Canadian government announced new sanctions Wednesday against several senior Iranian officials and state-run entities "for their role in the Iranian regime's brutal repression of its population."

The sanctions target five senior Iranian security and government officials and five state-run entities, the foreign ministry said in a statement, without providing specifics.

"These individuals and entities have contributed to Iran's efforts to suppress dissent and restrict fundamental freedoms of Iran's population, including through digital surveillance, censorship, unlawful violence, arbitrary detention and intimidation," the ministry said.

A protest movement in Iran sparked in late December by grievances over high living costs rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on Jan. 8 and 9.

Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths from the unrest, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Rights groups based abroad put the toll higher and accused security forces of firing at demonstrators.

Massive protests also erupted in Iran in Sep. 2022 following the death in custody of Iranian Kurdish woman Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested for allegedly violating strict dress rules for women.

UAE sanctions local branches of Iran's Bank Melli

The UAE central bank said Wednesday that it had imposed sanctions on the Emirati branches of Iran's Bank Melli, accusing it of violating local laws on money laundering, terrorism and arms proliferation.

The bank said in a statement that "it has been decided to prohibit all branches of Bank Melli Iran operating in the UAE from conducting any financial transactions to and from Iran, including trade finance and fund transfers."

It cited "non-compliance with the regulations, laws and supervisory decisions in force in the UAE, including the requirements and obligations set out under the legislation related to combating money laundering, the financing of terrorism and proliferation financing."

The announcement comes against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, as well as Washington's more recent economic pressure campaign against the Islamic Republic.

As part of that stepped-up campaign, the U.S. announced new measures at the end of August targeting Iran's trading partners, and sanctioned the director of the Dubai branch of Bank Melli.

Last month, the United Arab Emirates announced the suspension of trade and financial exchanges with Tehran.

German foreign minister: "Iran must engage constructively" in negotiations

Germany's foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, offered a direct criticism of Iranian negotiations in a meeting with his counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, on Tuesday at the U.N. General Assembly.

"Iran must engage constructively in talks for a sustainable solution to end the conflict in the region & unconditionally open the Strait of Hormuz, ensuring free, safe and toll-free navigation for all," he said on social media .

Wadephul's comments came as Iran continues to take a hard line in negotiations, demanding the U.S. remove its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, end the war on all fronts, release frozen or restricted assets and agree to the Oman-Iran negotiated passage through the strait, according to Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei .

Araghchi has yet to comment on the meeting with Wadephul, though the government shared photo of the two meeting on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.

Tehran reviewing U.S. response to its proposal, senior Iranian official tells Reuters

Iran is reviewing a U.S. response to its plan to end the fighting between the two countries, a senior Iranian official told the Reuters news agency on Wednesday, adding that many differences remain between the two sides.

The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the ending of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and vessels were subjects discussed during indirect talks with the U.S. on Tuesday, the official said.

Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei said Wednesday in a long interview aired by state television network IRIB that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the U.S. met Iran's long-stated conditions.

"There is no staging or step-by-step process," he said. "Iran is trying to have this implemented within three or four days, within four or five days, for example."

"The next step will also be determined and specified by the Islamic Republic of Iran," Rezaei said.

Iran has long demanded the U.S. lift its blockade and return to the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding signed in June by President Trump and his Iranian counterpart, which Tehran quickly accused the U.S. of breaching by keeping the blockade in place.

1 dead, 27 evacuated from vessel struck in Strait of Hormuz, Oman navy says

One crew member is dead and 27 others have been evacuated after a commercial vessel was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, Oman's royal navy said on social media , accompanied by a photo of the burning ship.

The crew member who was killed was a native of India, according to that country's Ministry of External Affairs . Twenty of the people on board the ship were Indian nationals, the agency said.

Oman identified the ship as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged merchant vessel Cape Dao.

The strike on a cargo vessel was reported earlier in the day by the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Center. The attack happened at about 7:30 a.m. local time.

The report from the UKMTO noted the ship was on fire and adrift, with Oman saying the ship was in the area of 2.5 nautical miles off the coast of the governorate of Musandam, which would correlate with the southern, U.S.-directed route through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian students return to schools and universities after war closures

Students in Iran returned to schools and universities Wednesday after months of closures due to the war with the United States, which has seen major attacks including a strike on the first day of the conflict that hit a school, killing about 150 people.

Parents walked hand-in-hand with their daughters, in mandatory headscarves and uniforms, as they arrived at a girls' primary school in western Tehran for the first day of the new academic year.

Classes were canceled after the U.S. and Israel jointly launched strikes on Iran, igniting the war, on Feb. 28. It was in that first wave of strikes that a school in the southern city of Minab was hit, leaving 120 children among the dead. A preliminary U.S. assessment not long after determined that American forces were "likely" responsible for the strike, though the school was not deliberately targeted.

In Minab on Wednesday, Iran's vice president for science and technology, Hossein Afshin, rang a bell at another primary school to signal the start of the new term. The bell-ringing, normally carried out by Iran's president, is part of traditional celebrations to welcome Iran's 16.5 million children back to school.

A ceremony featuring Masoud Pezeshkian was held two days early this year, before he left for the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

On Tuesday, a statement attributed to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei addressed the reopening, saying "the absence of some students, professors, and teachers" would be felt, referring to those killed during the conflict.

"This sorrow will guide our minds toward the true nature of the conflict between good and evil," the statement said.

U.S. soldier died in non-combat related incident en route to Mideast, defense official says

The U.S. Army has identified a soldier who died last week as a result of a non-combat related incident. A defense official told CBS News the soldier died due to a medical emergency while en route to the Middle East.

Capt. Bianca C. Wilkerson, 37, of Norfolk, Va., died on Sept. 18, 2026, according to a statement from the Army.

Wilkerson's death is counted on the Defense Casualty Analysis System under Overseas Operations , which brings the total number of U.S. military personnel killed during the war with Iran to 19. That tally includes deaths recorded by the Pentagon as occurring as part of Operation Epic Fury, the former name for the offensive against Iran, and under the broader Overseas Operations category.

Two additional non-combat U.S. personnel deaths that do not appear to be reflected in the DCAS system have been announced by the Pentagon, one of them a soldier supporting the ongoing U.S.-led mission against ISIS who died in "a training-related incident" in northern Iraq on May 31, and the other a New York National Guardsman who died of undetermined causes at Camp Buehring in Kuwait on March 6.

Iran president tells U.N. his country "victims of terrorism"

Iranian President Masoud Pezeskhian said in a Wednesday address to the United Nations General Assembly that his country had been a victim of terrorism, disputing President Trump's earlier accusation that Tehran was guilty of inflicting terror.

"We have been the victims of terrorism," Pezeshkian told world leaders gathered in New York. "I come from an Iran in which our esteemed supreme leader was assassinated without any legal framework or reason. I come from an Iran where, in truth, they bombed a school," he said, referring to strikes on a school in the southern city of Minab that killed about 170 people , mostly school girls between 7 and 12, on the first day of the war.

A preliminary U.S. assessment not long after determined that American forces were "likely" responsible for the strike, though the school was not deliberately targeted.

"Iran has never ever been an aggressor, has never started a war and has always shown her commitment to the negotiating table," Pezeshkian said. "They imposed the war on us, but we proved that we're not afraid of fighting."

Cargo vessel struck by unknown projectile in Strait of Hormuz, 2 casualties reported

A cargo vessel was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz Wednesday, leaving the vessel "on fire and adrift," according to a British military monitor.

"All crew have been evacuated with two casualties reported," the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said in a bulletin, adding that authorities were investigating the incident.

Vessel traffic through the strategic waterway has slowed to a crawl with Iran and the U.S. still quarreling over control of the strait.

At least 169 people killed in 3 days of fighting in Yemen

As many as 169 people have been reportedly killed in Yemen in the last three days as the Iran-aligned Houthis battle Saudi-backed government forces for control of strategic territory along the Red Sea coast, according to figures provided by both sides in the conflict.

Houthi military officials said at least 118 people had been killed in clashes as well as Saudi air and artillery strikes on Taiz, al-Jawf, Marib and Saada provinces since Sunday, the AFP news agency reported, while Yemeni government sources said at least 36 others had been killed.

According to the United Nations, at least 28 civilians have been killed and 82 injured since the latest escalation in Yemen began in August. The figure was reported by the U.N. Human Rights Office (OHCHR) and reiterated during a Sept. 22 U.N. Geneva briefing.

The U.N. stressed that it is not a comprehensive death toll and that the actual number is likely higher because access to information and verification remain severely restricted in Yemen.

Iranian flight lands in China despite U.S. sanctions threat, says tracker

A Mahan Air flight from Tehran landed in China's Guangzhou, tracking data by FlightRadar24 said on Wednesday, according to the AFP news agency, on the day Washington had threatened to "shut down" Tehran's carriers and punish anyone doing business with them.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned this week that any countries which provided Iranian planes with "landing services" would be "knocked out of the dollar system," but did not give further details.

The flight was not listed on the official website of Guangzhou Baiyun airport, which was the location shown as the landing site of the Mahan plane.

Iran's Civil Aviation Agency has said that flights from Tehran to Baghdad, Muscat and Ankara would be cancelled from Wednesday.

Around half of Iran's damaged South Pars gas field capacity restored, says official

Around 50% of the damaged production capacity at Iran's South Pars gas field has been restored, according to a senior oil ministry official cited by Iran's semi-official Fars news agency.

Ahmad Zeraatkar, Deputy Oil Minister for Planning, told Fars that efforts to restore production capacity began following damage to South Pars facilities early in the war, with some units back online ahead of schedule.

In March, Israel struck South Pars , part of the world's largest natural gas field, spiking global energy prices and drawing a rebuke from President Trump .

"By the end of September, around 50% of the damaged capacity had returned to service, and production in this section had resumed," Zeraatkar said.

Zeraatkar said the planned restoration targets had been achieved and that all scheduled measures would be completed before the start of winter.

He also called on consumers to help the effort by reducing energy consumption.

Countries suspend Iranian airline flights as U.S. sanctions take effect

Several countries began suspending flights operated by Iranian airlines to their airports on Wednesday as new U.S. sanctions targeting the country's aviation sector took effect.

The Trump administration announced earlier this month that Iran's entire air transport sector would be subject to sanctions. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that Iranian airlines would face difficulties operating globally from Sept. 23.

Georgia has banned flights operated by Iranian carriers from the country, while Iran's Mahan Air suspended flights to Turkey at Ankara's request .

Azerbaijan has also suspended Iranian flights, citing the new U.S. sanctions.

Iraq ordered the suspension of Iranian flights to Baghdad International Airport from Wednesday, according to the Reuters news agency. Iraqi authorities were, however, considering redirecting the flights to the central city of Najaf, an important Shiite Muslim pilgrimage destination.

"The decision does not mean a complete suspension of flights to Iraq, and that flights to other airports, including Najaf airport, will continue to operate as usual for all Iranian airlines," Iraqi Civil Aviation Organization spokesman Majid Akhavan said in remarks to Iranian media .

Iran's Civil Aviation Organization said flights from Tehran to Baghdad and Muscat , Oman, were canceled from Wednesday, while other remaining international flights, including those to Istanbul, would continue according to schedule.

It added that Iranian passengers were not being allowed to enter Oman's airport, with consultations underway on the issue.

Houthis threaten to target U.S. interests in Mideast if Washington intervenes in Yemen's civil war

The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen will attack U.S. interests in the Middle East if Washington intervenes in the conflict in support of Saudi Arabia, including by attempting to thwart Houthi efforts to blockade Saudi shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait , a military adviser for the group told the AFP news agency Wednesday.

"If America dares to intervene militarily with its fleets or tries to take control of Bab el-Mandeb, it is a red line for them and anyone else … we will fight over it," Houthi military adviser Abed Mohammed al-Thawr told the AFP.

The Houthis have dislodged Saudi-backed government forces from Yemen's Red Sea coast in recent weeks in fighting that has left hundreds dead. Houthi drones and missiles have also targeted Saudi sites, including the capital Riyadh, for the first time in years.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman requested help from President Trump in fighting the Houthis earlier in September, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. Yemen's government also made the request, a well-placed source told AFP.

The Houthis say Saudi Arabia has conducted hundreds of strikes in Yemen since fighting resumed in July, effectively ending a four-year truce.

"If America gambles on supporting Saudi Arabia with airstrikes or air support ... We will consider any American interests around us to be targets and we will not exclude anything," Thawr told AFP, adding that the group would "close Bab el-Mandeb completely to American ships."

Thawr denied receiving directives from Iran, but said they were "one alliance and one body."

"Iran is a friendly, allied, and brotherly country to us, but it does not direct us. We are independent in our decisions and in our sovereignty," he said.

Iran calls Trump's U.N. speech "a sign of desperation"

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei has said that President Trump's remarks to the U.N. were "a sign of desperation."

Speaking to state news agency IRNA, Baqaei also confirmed the talks held between U.S. and Iranian envoys on Tuesday took place via Qatari mediators.

"The Iranian delegation conveyed its views and its conditions very explicitly and clearly to the American side through the mediators," he said.

Addressing Mr. Trump's remarks about his pending "big decision" on whether to make a deal with, or "annihilate" the Iranian regime, Baqaei said: "The impression among diplomats and delegations from many countries here was that these remarks did not stem from strength, but from desperation … Threatening a country with military attack is an admission of the nature of the current U.S. ruling establishment."

U.S. and Iranian negotiators "successfully completed" indirect talks in NYC, Witkoff says

U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said American and Iranian negotiators "engaged in lengthy talks" on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

In a post on X late Tuesday, Witkoff said the two sides spoke through mediators over the course of the day. He did not describe the substance of the talks, but said they "successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising."

President Trump told reporters earlier Tuesday that Witkoff and U.S. envoy Jared Kushner had a "very good meeting," and the two sides "have another one scheduled in the very near future."

Trump meets with Gulf leaders on sidelines of U.N. General Assembly

President Trump joined a meeting of the Gulf Cooperation Council on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, where the president said there's a "lot of momentum" for Iran to make a deal. Countries represented in the meeting included Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Turkey.

"I like these people," the president said of the leaders around him.

The president said Iran's economy is in bad shape, and he hopes they do something good for their people.

"I don't think about the election at all when I think about ending the nuclear threat from Iran. I just think about ending the nuclear threat from Iran," he said.

U.S. delegation, including Kushner and Witkoff, met with Iranian officials, Trump says

President Trump said U.S. and Iranian officials met on Tuesday, shortly after threatening in his address to the U.N. General Assembly that he may "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal isn't reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.

Mr. Trump told reporters the meeting happened, and ended "about an hour ago," but offered few details about the talks.

"It was a very good meeting," Mr. Trump said. "They have another one scheduled in the very near future."

The meeting lasted about three hours, Mr. Trump said, and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and special envoy Steve Witkoff were part of it.

Witkoff echoed that the meeting went well, saying "I feel very good right now," but provided no further details.

Iran and U.S. held peace talks Tuesday, Trump says

The U.S. and Iran held talks Tuesday while both countries are at the U.N. for this week's General Assembly, President Trump said. He also said he believes the U.S. will come to an agreement with Iran, though he did not specify when.

"I think that a settlement is going to be reached," Mr. Trump said during a bilateral meeting with U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham. "They want to talk to us. They have been talking to us. Even today, they've been talking to us, and the relationship is developing, let's say."

Mr. Trump was not more specific about what he meant by the "relationship is developing," or put a time frame on when the agreement would come. Earlier in the day, however, he expected the deal to come after the midterm elections.

The president also seemed to say Iran had agreed that it would not pursue a nuclear weapon.

"They understand that we can't let them have a nuclear weapon, and there's a price to pay for that," Mr. Trump said.

The Iranian delegation is expected in New York City for the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, though it's not yet clear whether Mr. Trump will meet with either their president or foreign minister.

Trump says deciding between deal or driving Iran "into hell"

President Trump told the United Nations General Assembly Tuesday that he had to choose whether to "annihilate" Iran if it fails to make a deal to end the Iran war.

"I have a big decision to make – will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?" Mr. Trump said.

"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" he said. "Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"

The president also reiterated that he believes an agreement is possible before U.S. midterm elections in November, in which his Republican Party faces losing control of Congress at least partly due to high fuel prices caused by the war.

"I believe we'll make a deal right after the election because it doesn't make sense for them not to," he said.

"They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don't realize is that I'm not running. I did that already, and won in a landslide," he said.

Mr. Trump said Sunday he would "probably" meet on the sidelines of the U.N. summit with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is attending along with the country's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

articles.title: Dirty tricks: Why is Congress voting to scrap California’s clean air protections?
articles.summary: This congressional overstep is creating an alarming precedent, threatening states’ authority to protect their residents from toxic pollution. The Senate must step in to stop it.
articles.body:
Just last week, the U.S. House of Representatives voted to revoke a federal waiver that allows California to protect its residents from cancer-causing pollution released by ships , most of them foreign, docking at the state’s ports.

Americans should understand just how reckless this is — and why the consequences extend beyond California.

The waiver allows California to enforce its Ocean-Going Vessels At-Berth Regulation . In plain terms, the program requires ships to stop pumping toxic diesel exhaust, proven to cause detrimental health outcomes, into the air while they are docked.

These shipping companies have valid solutions available. They can plug into shore power (the electric grid) and turn off their engines, or they can use technology that captures pollutants before they reach nearby communities.

Even when a ship is not moving, it typically keeps diesel-powered auxiliary engines running to supply electricity for lights, ventilation, pumps, refrigeration and other onboard systems. A vessel may remain at a port for hours or even days, releasing soot and smog-forming gases close to homes, schools and workplaces.

That pollution is not harmless. Diesel exhaust is known to the State of California to cause cancer , while exposure to air pollution is also linked to asthma, heart and lung disease, cognitive decline and premature death. The microscopic particles in diesel exhaust can travel deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

The health burden is especially severe in communities surrounding California’s busiest ports. In a 2022 survey of Wilmington residents , 54 percent reported black spots or oily residue around their homes, and 57 percent reported respiratory ailments in their households.

California created its at-berth program to stop this pollution before it reaches the air. And the program is working.

The original program achieved an 80 percent reduction in harmful emissions across more than 13,000 vessel visits beginning in 2014. California later expanded the program to cover additional vessels, including auto carriers and tankers — categories responsible for 56 percent of the fine-particle pollution produced by ocean-going vessels while docked at California ports.

The projected public health benefits of this program are substantial. Once fully implemented, California’s program is expected to reduce pollution from vessel visits by 90 percent and lower the potential cancer risk by 55 percent for communities near the ports of Los Angeles, Long Beach and Richmond. California estimates that it will deliver $2.31 billion in public health benefits.

The infrastructure has already been built. Ports, utilities and private businesses have invested. Shore-power connections and approved emissions capture systems are already operating, allowing ships to reduce their pollution without disrupting the movement of goods.

The primary argument for taking away California’s waiver has been cost. Opponents have cited large total figures to suggest the program places a significant burden on everyday Americans. But those numbers obscure what compliance actually costs when spread across the enormous quantities of goods these ships carry.

According to the federal government’s own analysis , the cost is approximately $1.14 for each shipping container, $7.66 for each automobile transported and less than 1 cent for each gallon of finished product carried by a tanker.

For context, a 20-foot shipping container holds goods worth approximately $54,500 on average . The $1.14 compliance cost amounts to roughly two-thousandths of a penny for every dollar of goods inside.

Taking away California’s waiver would therefore produce no meaningful savings for consumers. It would instead shift the far greater costs of pollution from international shipping and oil companies onto California families, workers and taxpayers through preventable illness, missed work and higher health care expenses.

On the House floor, lawmakers also argued that oil tankers cannot connect to shore power. But that leaves out a critical fact: California’s program does not require every ship to use shore power. When plugging in is not practical, vessels can use state-approved emissions capture and control technology instead. In fact, major oil companies are currently using the technology at California ports. Shell and Olympus Terminals are among the companies already being served in Southern California, while TransMontaigne has signed an agreement to use the technology at its Martinez and Richmond terminals.

The infrastructure exists. The technology works. Companies are using it. Goods continue moving through California’s ports without disruption. And the cost to consumers is negligible.

Now the decision falls to the Senate. Senators can defend a proven program that reduces cancer risk, protects communities and respects investments already made by California businesses, or they can make it easier for ships to keep pumping toxic exhaust into our air.

Californians should be watching. Senators who claim to care about public health must reject this measure and preserve California’s waiver.

Dori Chandler is a policy advocate with the Coalition for Clean Air working to protect communities from pollution caused by heavy-duty freight and shipping.

articles.title: On the Ballot: 10 GOP House seats most likely to flip in November
articles.summary: With less than six weeks to go until November’s elections, Republicans are on defense as the midterm landscape looks increasingly favorable for Democrats. Forecasters including Sabato’s Crystal Ball and Fox News have shifted House races away from Republicans in recent weeks, signaling an increasingly tough terrain for the party to hold on to its 218-seat…
articles.body:
With less than six weeks to go until November’s elections, Republicans are on defense as the midterm landscape looks increasingly favorable for Democrats.

Forecasters including Sabato’s Crystal Ball and Fox News have shifted House races away from Republicans in recent weeks, signaling an increasingly tough terrain for the party to hold on to its 218-seat majority, despite redistricting efforts to stem their losses.

As President Trump’s approval rating tumbles, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) now forecasts that Democrats, who need to net at least four seats to win the House, have a 72 percent probability of flipping the lower chamber — and a 52 percent chance of taking both chambers.

Ratings are changing quickly, and forecasters differ in just how competitive they consider the country’s top races. Here are 10 of the Republican-held House seats that are most likely to flip in November.

Rep. David Schweikert (R-Ariz.) left his seat for an unsuccessful gubernatorial run, giving Democrats a unique pickup opportunity in the Phoenix-area suburbs. Democrat Amish Shah, a former state lawmaker and emergency medicine doctor, is running against Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker for the Arizona Cardinals.

This House match-up is unique in that the pair previously worked for the same team: Feely played for the New York Jets while Shah was a team doctor.

The district went for Trump by 3 percentage points in 2024 , yet the minority party has a strong chance to flip the House seat with no incumbent and favorable political winds for Democrats.

DDHQ forecasts that the seat leans Democrat, while Cook Political Report rates it as a toss-up.

Rep. Juan Ciscomani (R-Ariz.) is no stranger to tough races for this Tucson-area House seat. He defeated Democrat Kirsten Engel by just more than a point in 2022, and he defeated her again in 2024 by more than 2 points.

This cycle, he faces Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran. On the campaign trail, Ciscomani has pointed out that he’s been ranked as Arizona’s most bipartisan House member and touted the tax cuts from Republicans’ tax cut and spending megabill.

Meanwhile, Mendoza argues that Ciscomani’s votes supporting tariffs and the megabill are making life worse for Arizonans. Trump narrowly won Ciscomani’s seat in 2024 by less than a point.

DDHQ rates Ciscomani’s seat as “likely Democrat” while Cook rates the seat a toss-up.

After Democrats successfully redrew California’s congressional lines, Rep. David Valadao’s (R-Calif.) Central Valley district will offer a key test of whether the blue-friendly redistricting effort pays off.

Valadao served in the House for three terms before he narrowly lost reelection in 2018’s blue-wave midterms, but he went on to win back his seat in 2020. A moderate, he was among the small handful of Republicans who voted for Trump’s second impeachment.

Valadao won his sixth term by roughly 7 points in 2024, but sparse polling has signaled a potentially closer contest against Democrat Randy Villegas this year.

DDHQ considers it a likely Democratic race, while Cook rates it a toss-up.

Republican Rep. Don Bacon is retiring in Nebraska’s “blue dot” district, opening up a competitive race in Omaha.

Democratic businesswoman Denise Powell and Omaha City Council member Brinker Harding (R) are squaring off for a seat that has gone red every cycle since 2016, despite voting blue in the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections.

Cook considers the district to lean Democratic, while DDHQ rates it a step closer to being solidly blue.

Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R-N.J.) is seeking a third term in Washington after a months-long absence from Congress this year.

When Kean returned to Capitol Hill in late June after missing more than 100 House votes, he revealed that he’d been treated for depression, but his hiatus from the House sparked scrutiny and has made him one of the chambers most vulnerable Republican incumbents.

Kean, the son of popular former New Jersey Gov. Thomas Kean (R), defeated former Rep. Tom Malinowski (D-N.J.) by 3 points in the 2022 midterms.

DDHQ now gives former Navy helicopter pilot Rebecca Bennett (D) an 80 percent chance of winning the district, which Trump won by just more than a point in 2024.

Virginia Democrats tried and failed to redistrict the state this year, with a court striking down a voter-approved measure that would have given the party a boost in the House.

Now, former Rep. Elaine Luria (D) is challenging Rep. Jen Kiggans (R) in a rematch, after Kiggans unseated Luria back in 2022.

Like New Jersey’s 7th District, Cook considers the race a toss-up, while DDHQ rates it as likely Democratic.

The third time could be the charm for Democrat Christina Bohannan, who hopes to oust Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa) in red Iowa.

After winning the district in 2020, Miller-Meeks fended off a challenge from Bohannan by around 7 points in 2022, then scraped through two years later in a rematch , winning by less than one-fifth of a point as Trump won the district by 8.5 points in the presidential race.

Now, sparse polling has shown Bohannan several points ahead of the Trump-backed incumbent, who notably voted with Democrats last week for a resolution seen as a rebuke of Trump’s moves in Iran.

DDHQ considers the race likely Democratic, while Cook rates it as a toss-up.

Another rematch is underway in Wisconsin’s 3rd District, where Democrat Rebecca Cooke is running again after coming just 2 points shy of ousting Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) in 2024.

An outspoken Trump ally who attended the Jan. 6, 2021, rally ahead of the U.S. Capitol attack, Van Orden has leaned into his support for Trump in the battleground district the president won three times.

Meanwhile, the incumbent is putting pressure on Cooke, a former board member of the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation, for declining to debate .

Cook rates the race as a toss-up, and DDHQ rates it as “lean Democratic.”

The Centennial State gained a new seat after the 2020 census reapportionment. The seat covers the northern suburbs of Denver and stretches all the way through Greeley.

A true toss-up — it went for Trump by less than 2 points in 2024 — the district has swung between Democratic and Republican control. Former Rep. Yadira Caraveo (D-Colo.) won the seat in 2022, but the district later changed hands when Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colo.) won in 2024.

Now Evans is running against former state Rep. Manny Rutinel (D) for the House seat, and the district could very well change hands again.

DDHQ rates the race for Evans’s seat as “likely Democrat” while Cook calls it a toss-up.

Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pa.) flipped his Pennsylvania district by roughly 4,000 votes in 2024, and challenger Bob Brooks (D) hopes he can flip the seat back this fall.

Brooks, a firefighter union president, has cast himself as a champion of the working class in a district that went to Trump by 3 points in 2024, amid growing frustration with the president’s handling of the economy.

But Mackenzie’s race got a recent fundraising jolt from tech mogul Elon Musk’s super PAC. Kiggans, Kean and Van Orden also snagged the billionaire’s support.

The Pennsylvania race is another Cook toss-up, while DDHQ considers it to lean toward Democrats.

articles.title: States should adopt the federal rule that keeps junk science out of criminal courts
articles.summary: It empowers judges to act as gatekeepers, preventing speculative science from reaching juries or being admitted in the discovery process.
articles.body:
After 37 years behind bars, Robert Wallace Lyons, convicted of murdering Lori Stabenow in a Eugene, Ore. motel room, has been released from prison . Though he is not yet a free man in the fullest sense, prosecutors are deciding whether to retry him.

In 1990, a Lane County jury found Lyons guilty of killing Stabenow, who was discovered strangled in her room at the Stage Stop Inn. The case against him relied heavily on bitemark evidence, a forensic technique whereby an expert compares marks on a victim’s body to a suspect’s teeth. Once widely accepted in courtrooms, this methodology has since been debunked due to its failure to produce scientifically reliable results.

In Lyons’s case, bitemark evidence was the centerpiece of the state’s case. A forensic odontologist testified he had no doubt that marks found on Stabenow’s body matched wax molds made from Lyons’ teeth. That testimony helped secure a conviction that stood for decades until Oregon passed a law this year formally recognizing bitemark analysis as a discredited forensic discipline. That opened the door for Lyons and others convicted on similar evidence to challenge their cases.

As forensic science has evolved, bitemark evidence and the “direct comparison” methodology used by forensic dentists have since been widely rejected , raising serious questions about convictions that relied on such evidence.

Lyons is finally seeing some form of justice, but other individuals who have spent years on death row due to faulty evidence in their cases deserve another perspective as well. Oregon had no judicial gatekeeping standard in place and still doesn’t, illustrating what can happen to people like Lyons when courts fail to rigorously enforce it.

That is where one key federal rule of evidence known as Rule 702 comes in handy, empowering judges to act as gatekeepers and preventing speculative science from reaching juries or being admitted in the discovery process. It helps judges weed out manufactured evidence before it can skew a verdict. It’s an important standard, one that protects against runaway outcomes and safeguards just verdicts in criminal cases where the death penalty is on the line. While it directly governs the federal court system, it has served as a decades-long blueprint for states to adopt similar rigorous standards in their own evidentiary rules.

This is exactly why rigorous evidentiary standards matter. They ensure courtroom outcomes are decided by hard facts, not faulty claims that can cost an innocent person their freedom.

But in Lyon’s case, the problem wasn’t just a lack of gatekeeping standards, but how long it took to revisit it once those standards caught up with the science. Bitemark analysis was deemed unreliable in 2009 , yet it took another 17 years for Lyon to be released on bond.

Bitemark analysis, arson pattern evidence and bullet lead composition analysis are just a few of the forensic techniques that have secured convictions in courts with unenforced gatekeeping standards, only to be discredited later. With no consistent standard to ensure these techniques don’t creep into verdicts, many people still risk facing jail time for crimes they did not commit.

States that have not yet aligned their admissibility standards with federal standards should take the steps to do so. Ensuring that expert testimony is rooted in science rather than speculation should be a priority nationwide. Without that uniformity, we’re left with a fragmented judicial system where the outcome of a case, even a capital punishment case, can depend on the location of the trial rather than the facts.

No appellate process can undo an execution or a lifetime is prison, like the one Robert Wallace Lyons is hoping to narrowly escape. Irreversibility is exactly why gatekeeping has to work upfront, not just on review years or decades later.

How many other convictions built on the same discredited tactics are still standing? How many people have been sentenced to death because of weak expert witness standards? These are questions with real answers. The solution is not a mystery. States need to align their standards with federal rules before the next Robert Wallace Lyons runs out of time.

David Safavian is an attorney, conservative activist and chief operating officer of Unify.US. Jason Pye is vice president of the Due Process Institute.

articles.title: Collins leads Maine Senate race by 3 points: Survey
articles.summary: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) leads Democrat Troy Jackson by 3 points in her bid for a sixth term, according to a new poll. The New York Times/Siena University survey found Collins leading Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate, with 49 percent support to the Democrat’s 46 percent. The incumbent’s edge was within the…
articles.body:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) leads Democrat Troy Jackson by 3 points in her bid for a sixth term, according to a new poll.

The New York Times/Siena University survey found Collins leading Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate, with 49 percent support to the Democrat’s 46 percent.

The incumbent’s edge was within the roughly 5 point margin of error, while another 5 percent of the 619 respondents were undecided, the results show.

Jackson led Collins by 9 points among women, 18 points among respondents aged 30-44 and by 34 points among Hispanics in the survey. Men, respondents aged 45-64, white and Black respondents backed the incumbent over the Democratic hopeful by 16, 19, 6 and 18 points, respectively.

As of Wednesday, Decision Desk HQ gave Jackson a 54 percent chance to win the race, which is crucial for Democrats’ chances of retaking the upper chamber of Congress. The party needs to flip a net of four seats for a majority in the Senate.

Jackson replaced Graham Platner on the ballot in July , after the oyster farmer dropped out of the race amid allegations of sexual assault — which he denied.

A progressive who lost the Democratic gubernatorial primary in June to former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree, Jackson has campaigned on “Medicare for All,” abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and raising taxes on billionaires and corporations.

He has also aligned Collins with President Trump, who lost Maine in all three of his presidential campaigns. But the GOP senator broke with the president multiple times over the summer, criticizing his tariff war with Canada and voting against Attorney General Todd Blanche’s confirmation.

Collins, along with Maine Sen. Angus King (I), who caucuses with Democrats, also urged the Senate Commerce Committee last week to take up House-passed legislation that would extend a pause on whaling regulations.

Maine lobster industry leaders have championed the bill , which is titled the Northeast Lobstermen Protection Act and sponsored by outgoing Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) in the lower chamber.

The Times/Siena poll was conducted from Sept. 15-22 in collaboration with the Portland Press Herald and was sponsored in part by the Maine Trust for Local News.

articles.title: Reopen America’s golden door to refugees fleeing religious persecution
articles.summary: The fiscal year that ends later this month will be the first year on record in which no Christians fleeing religious persecution were resettled as refugees in the U.S.
articles.body:
At the end of each fiscal year, the president, in consultation with Congress and various agencies, determines the annual federal ceiling for refugee resettlement. Each year, the ceiling is set by weighing the current global refugee needs, U.S. foreign policy interests, domestic labor needs and the U.S.’s commitment to international religious liberty.

Historically, refugee resettlement has been an opportunity to exercise soft power, build international goodwill and bolster essential gaps in our workforce. The U.S. has resettled an average of 73,500 refugees a year since the creation of the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program in 1980, with some years seeing a ceiling as high as 200,000. It has also been a key mechanism to underscore the U.S.’s commitment to protecting those persecuted for their faith abroad.

Fiscal 2026 changed all of that. In a drastic change of U.S. government’s policy towards refugees — individuals who have fled a well-founded fear of persecution in the country of origin for specific reasons, including their religion — the fiscal 2026 Presidential Determination on Refugee Admissions was set at an unprecedented low, just 7,500 spots . Even with a mid-year increase to 17,500 , this is still the lowest final refugee ceiling since the resettlement program was established.

More startling than the number itself was its demographic designation. Rather than continuing to allow refugees already in the pipeline — who demonstrated a credible fear on account of race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular group — continue through the process, the administration almost entirely restricted these spots to white South Africans .

Since South Africa is not known for religious persecution toward the majority Christian population or religious minorities, the sole focus on South African nationals has necessarily meant excluding refugees persecuted on account of their religion.

Only three refugees were resettled to the U.S. in fiscal 2026 from among the 50 countries on the World Watch List for Christian persecution created by Open Doors (one of us leads Open Doors US) and none were religious minorities. In fact, the fiscal year that ends later this month will be the first year on record in which no Christians fleeing religious persecution were resettled as refugees in the U.S.

Unfortunately, this year also saw persecuted Christians who had already been resettled lawfully in the U.S. experience new challenges. In January, the Department of Homeland Security re-interviewed lawfully present refugees who had applied for but not yet received their green cards. Christian refugees from countries known for persecution, like Burma, were detained, separated from their children and transferred to detention centers in Texas.

Though the courts have for the moment halted further such detentions of lawfully resettled refugees, the policy has retraumatized people who have already survived unthinkable tragedies.

All this has occurred as the circumstances facing refugees and persecuted Christians have only grown more dire. Over 41 million people were refugees at the end of 2025, among the over 117 million people who have had to flee their homes for violence, conflict or other reasons.

Meanwhile, over 388 million Christians around the world face high levels of persecution and discrimination. Although only a fraction of these Christians will end up fleeing their home countries for safety in a second or third country, some of the countries producing the most refugees are also known for extreme persecution of Christians, including Iran, Syria and Afghanistan.

Americans across the political spectrum have watched these developments over the last two years with growing concern. Among evangelical Christians , 70 percent believe that the U.S. has a moral responsibility to accept refugees. Among evangelical pastors , 78 percent agree, with just 2 percent saying that no refugees should be resettled to the U.S. Eighty-seven percent say those persecuted for their Christian faith should be a priority for resettlement, while just 20 percent say the same of the South African population who are currently the sole priority.

Setting the annual Presidential Determination on Refugee Admissions is particularly weighty during an election year. Midterm elections are moments of self-reflection, both for the administration in power and the nation as a whole.

With regards to their approach to Christian refugees, we believe the government has an opportunity to recalibrate their policies to match the humane standards that most Americans, including most evangelical Christians, value. The president could do so simply by ensuring that his fiscal 2027 refugee determination precisely echoes the prioritization for those fleeing religious persecution that was a hallmark of his first term.

We desperately need to recognize that every day we wait enables further mistreatment of some of our most vulnerable brothers and sisters in Christ. Even before we get to November, the administration and lawmakers from both parties should commit to reform our border and asylum processes in ways that preserve security while ensuring that those persecuted for their faith continue to have access to the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program.

Ryan Brown is the president and CEO of Open Doors US. Myal Greene is the president and CEO of World Relief.

articles.title: Young men are swinging away hard from Republicans, pessimistic about economy, new poll finds
articles.summary: A new poll shows congressional Democrats with a growing lead among young men, who list cost-of-living issues as their top concern.
articles.body:
Republicans' 2024 gains among young men have evaporated — and that could have instant ramifications this November, according to a new Cygnal poll .

President Donald Trump narrowly carried young men in 2024, according to exit polls , a big swing toward the GOP from past elections. But Democrats' generic ballot lead among men ages 18-30 who say they are the most determined to vote now sits at 57%-40%, according to the poll.

Trump's favorability is underwater at just 38%-55%, and Republicans' net favorability among the demographic now sits at -9 points, with 40% viewing the party favorably and 49% unfavorably.

One silver lining for the GOP: Among all registered voters sampled, including those least likely to turn out in November, the Democratic generic ballot lead is much smaller, 44% to 41%.

"It is not a very good electorate, if you're the Republican Party, among the people who are the most determined to vote," said Alex Tarascio, pollster and principal at Cygnal, in an interview with POLITICO ahead of the poll's release during Thursday's Symposium on Young American Men.

Young men alone likely won't determine control of Congress; they make up a fraction of the electorate, and they are less likely to vote than women of the same age or their older counterparts. But that lack of enthusiasm itself is a warning sign for Republicans, who will need to motivate their base ahead of November if they wish to maintain control of Congress.

The young men sampled are overwhelmingly concerned about cost-of-living issues — the same reason that many swung toward the GOP two years ago.

When given a list of options and asked which will matter most in determining their vote in November, a wide plurality — 29% — selected "inflation and the cost of living," and another 14% chose "housing costs and being able to afford a place to live." When asked what policies would make the biggest difference in their lives, the top answers again deal with the economy: The most-selected options were lowering the cost of goods, lowering housing costs and cutting taxes.

Many young men feel pessimistic about their ability to achieve success. When asked if they feel the rules in this country are set up to work for or against young men, 43% said they feel the rules are set up against them to 47% who said the rules are set up in their favor.

That pessimism bleeds into how they view other institutions. Both the Democratic Party (-1) and Republican Party (-9) have net-negative favorability among the demographic, and the White House's current occupants are even more unpopular: Vice President JD Vance sits at 37% favorability with -10 net favorability, while Trump is at 38% favorability with -17 net.

"Young men are pretty down on institutions and political figures, and this one isn't any exception to that," Tarascio said.

Republicans successfully targeted young men and low-propensity voters in 2024 to help propel them to victory largely in part by having Trump sit for interviews with podcast hosts and influencers popular with young men. Trump has yet to return to those forums en masse ahead of the midterms, but he's repeatedly told voters to pretend as if he's on the ballot in November.

But Trump may no longer be the motivator he once was for turning out young, male, low-propensity voters. Among those surveyed who were least likely to vote, Trump's net favorability is -22, lower than the respondents most likely to vote, where his net favorability is -19.

"If Trump gets in front of them, I don't think it's a bad bet, but for some of these people it could backfire," Tarascio said.

The poll was conducted Sept. 15-18 with a sample of 800 registered male voters ages 18-30. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.46 percentage points.

CORRECTION: A previous version of this article misstated that this poll had a likely voter screen. Democrats have a 57%-40% lead among men ages 18-30 who say they're the most determined to vote.

articles.title: Democrats leading in Michigan, New Hampshire Senate races: Survey
articles.summary: Democrats are maintaining their leads in the U.S. Senate races in Michigan and New Hampshire, according to New York Times/Siena polling released Thursday. In the Michigan race, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed garnered 49 percent support compared with the 44 percent of respondents who favored Republican Mike Rogers. The Democrat has maintained a slight lead over…
articles.body:
Democrats are maintaining their leads in the U.S. Senate races in Michigan and New Hampshire, according to New York Times/Siena polling released Thursday.

In the Michigan race, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed garnered 49 percent support compared with the 44 percent of respondents who favored Republican Mike Rogers. The Democrat has maintained a slight lead over his GOP opponent in polling this month.

In New Hampshire, Democrat Chris Pappas also posted a 5-point advantage in the state’s Senate race, receiving 50 percent support compared with the 45 percent backing earned by Republican candidate John Sununu.

Both New Hampshire candidates received net-negative favorability ratings of minus 1 point from voters. Independent voters, a key voting bloc in the state, leaned toward supporting Pappas by 10 points.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins pulled ahead in a separate survey conducted on Maine’s Senate race, garnering a 3-point advantage over Democratic challenger Troy Jackson.

Jackson had a narrow lead on the incumbent senator in polling from CNN and YouGov earlier this month, but this new survey could raise GOP hopes for maintaining control of the vulnerable Senate seat.

Voters surveyed in all three states also indicated dissatisfaction with President Trump, with 63 percent expressing disapproval of how he has handled his job as president.

The president’s approval ratings, particularly regarding his management of the economy, have taken a hit in polling since the outbreak of the Iran war earlier this year. When asked specifically about how Trump has handled economic issues as president, 65 percent of survey respondents said they either strongly or somewhat disapproved of his approach to the issue.

A large share, or 40 percent, of the respondents identified as independent voters. Of these voters, 50 percent said they leaned more toward the Democratic Party and 39 percent said they leaned toward the Republican Party.

The New York Times/Siena polls were conducted from Sept. 15 to 22 among 619 Maine voters, 605 Michigan voters and 613 New Hampshire voters. The margin of error was approximately 4.9 percentage points in each state and 2.8 percentage points for the collective results.

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico journalists unable to access White House despite judge’s order
articles.summary: CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters were unable to access the White House on Thursday, despite a federal judge ordering the Trump administration to immediately restore their press credentials. CNN reporter Betsy Klein and a photojournalist were also denied access to the White House grounds early Thursday, while one CNN producer was able to enter…
articles.body:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters were unable to access the White House on Thursday, despite a federal judge ordering the Trump administration to immediately restore their press credentials.

CNN reporter Betsy Klein and a photojournalist were also denied access to the White House grounds early Thursday, while one CNN producer was able to enter the property using their pass, the outlet reported .

“There was no reason provided for the refusal and CNN will continue to try to gain access as regular business hours start,” CNN’s story on the matter noted.

MS NOW also noted on its website that its reporter was blocked from the White House after the court ruling came in overnight.

A Politico reporter, meanwhile, “was denied access” to the White House on Thursday, and his press credentials were “confiscated,” according to the organization.

The journalists were blocked from the grounds before 9 a.m. EDT. Given the timing, there is a possibility the ruling was not yet processed.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled early Thursday that the White House must grant reporters from the blocked outlets access to the White House complex, days after the media organizations sued after President Trump banned their journalists from his residence.

The ruling from Kelly , a Trump appointee, lasts for two weeks. In his emergency ruling, the judge wrote the reporters “did not receive an opportunity to be heard” before the White House revoked their credentials.

“Moreover, Plaintiffs — and the public — have an abiding interest in maintaining the status quo ante given the importance of the free press, which ‘stands as one of the great interpreters between the government and the people,’” he added in the eight-page ruling.

Theodore Boutrous, an attorney for the outlets, called Kelly’s decision a “strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law.”

Boutrous later on Thursday morning wrote to the court asking for an emergency hearing on the matter “as soon as possible,” saying the outlets’ legal team had reached out to DOJ attorneys and had not heard back.

“And time is of the essence —CNN is scheduled to be the television pool this evening for President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House,” Boutrous wrote. “Defendants have already repeatedly violated the Court’s Order.”

The White House has not commented on the judge’s late-night decision; while Trump made a series of Truth Social posts early Thursday but did not acknowledge the judge’s ruling in any of them.

articles.title: Democrats lead in Texas Senate, gubernatorial race: Poll
articles.summary: A new poll shows Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa leading their Republican opponents ahead of the 2026 midterm elections in November. In the Marist Poll, Talarico garnered 50 percent support, while Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) received 44 percent. Four percent of respondents remained undecided, and 2 percent…
articles.body:
A new poll shows Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa leading their Republican opponents ahead of the 2026 midterm elections in November.

In the Marist Poll , Talarico garnered 50 percent support, while Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) received 44 percent. Four percent of respondents remained undecided, and 2 percent chose another candidate.

For the gubernatorial race, Hinojosa had 49 percent support and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) had 46 percent. Three percent of respondents were undecided and 1 percent chose another candidate.

Talarico and Hinojosa led among independents, at 55 percent and 52 percent, respectively. Even with their leads, when respondents were asked who they thought would win each race, 52 percent said they think Paxton will win the Senate race and 68 percent said they believe Abbott will be reelected.

Despite Democrats usually facing an uphill battle in the Lone Star State, the Cook Political Report has shifted the Senate race to a “ toss-up ” while the gubernatorial race shifted to “ likely Republican ” in August.

The shifts in Democrats’ favor occurred after Hinojosa launched ads attacking Abbott for accepting money from data centers — an issue that has taken center stage this election cycle.

Abbott rescinded his past support of Texas data center projects this election cycle, telling voters he called for blocking new development in rural parts of Texas. He has also asked state regulators to ensure residents are not “burdened” with data center-related infrastructure costs.

If Abbott wins in November, he will become the longest-serving governor in the state’s history and continue a 30-year streak of Republicans holding the office.

Paxton, meanwhile, has divided Texas voters with his past scandals, including previously facing impeachment in the Texas state House on corruption charges before being acquitted in the state Senate.

GOP groups — such as the Senate Leadership Fund’s Texas affiliate tied to Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) — are starting to pour money into the race, which is key to Republican hopes of maintaining Senate control.

This Marist survey of 1,139 registered voters in Texas was conducted Sept. 17 to 20. The margin of error was 4.4 percentage points.
