articles.title: Why Trump should designate Ecuador as a major non-NATO ally
articles.summary: Under President Daniel Noboa, Ecuador has restored extradition and expanded military, intelligence and law-enforcement cooperation with Washington.
articles.body:
The Trump administration’s National Security Strategy calls for restoring “American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere” by enlisting “regional champions” to stop drug flows and “neutralize cartels.” No country has put that strategy into practice more clearly than Ecuador. Under President Daniel Noboa, Ecuador has restored extradition and expanded military, intelligence and law-enforcement cooperation with Washington.

The U.S. should reward this cooperation and lay the groundwork for deepening it further by designating Ecuador as a major non-NATO ally.

Ecuador’s partnership has proven to be especially valuable at sea. Since Ecuadorian and American forces launched joint operations in March, the U.S. Coast Guard cutter James was able to conduct nine interdictions and seize more than 46,500 pounds of narcotics. Last month, Quito announced that two U.S. warships would patrol Ecuadorian waters. Three Black Hawk helicopters were already in Manta and are now poised to conduct additional operations. Together, those air and naval assets add American reach to operations Ecuador is already helping us carry out.

Extradition offers even stronger proof of Ecuador’s commitment to the new American security doctrine. After Ecuadorian voters approved extradition in transnational organized crime cases by a margin of nearly 30 percent in a referendum, Ecuador sent three of its own nationals accused of major narcotics offenses to American courts.

Jose Adolfo Macias Villamar (aka “Fito”), the leader of the criminal group Los Choneros , became the first Ecuadorian national extradited by Ecuador to the U.S. under the 2024 reform. Two more Ecuadorian nationals accused of international drug trafficking followed this June. Cartel leaders now know that an arrest in Ecuador can end in an American jail cell, which is a prerequisite for long-term success against cartel leadership.

Ecuador’s courts have also shown that they can prosecute both cartel finance and abuses by the country’s own security forces. An Ecuadorian tribunal convicted six people and two companies for laundering more than $17 million through Macias Villamar’s family network. In a separate case, a trial court convicted 16 servicemen of the forced disappearance of four boys (three of those convicted have filed appeals ). Ecuador can balance a stringent crackdown on criminal groups with domestic accountability, which makes it a reliable partner.

Major non-NATO ally status would put that partnership on firmer footing. It would not create a NATO-style promise to defend Ecuador or write Quito a blank check. Instead, it would make Ecuador eligible for military training on reciprocal terms, cooperative defense research and testing and loans of materials or equipment for those joint projects.

If Washington later provides military financing for an approved purchase, Quito could contract directly with an American defense firm. Used well, those authorities could improve maritime surveillance and aircraft maintenance, enhance secure communications and boost the ability of Ecuadorian and American forces to work together. The designation would make long-term cooperation easier to plan and help turn today’s deployments into lasting Ecuadorian capacity.

The designation also makes strategic sense given Ecuador’s location. Colombia is already a major non-NATO ally, and President Trump designated Peru in January. Ecuador lies between them on the Andean Pacific coast.

Giving all three the same status could make it easier for Washington to train their forces to work together and develop joint defense projects along a principal cocaine corridor. It would also show the hemisphere that Washington rewards governments that align with the United States and is willing to help them weather the short-term costs that come with confronting criminal groups more forcefully after years of resigned neglect.

Five House Republicans, led by Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), have already urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio to support the designation. President Trump can act without negotiating a treaty, and the statutory process requires him to notify Congress at least 30 days before designation but does not require Congress to approve the designation with a vote.

The administration has asked the region for governments willing to confront the cartels, share the burden of creating a secure hemisphere and align openly and unapologetically with the United States. Ecuador has answered that call. Designating it a major non-NATO ally would give the phrase “regional champion” concrete meaning and give other governments a reason to follow Ecuador’s lead.

Gil Guerra is a fellow at Hudson Institute and a contributing writer at The Dispatch. He specializes in politics, security, and technology in Latin America and the Caribbean.

articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday dismissed a report that alleged his administration pushed to include his name on Ford’s Theatre, calling it “a ridiculous lie.” “The story that the White House, or me, want to affix my name to Ford’s Theatre, in Washington, D.C., where Abraham Lincoln was assassinated, is a ridiculous lie. articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday dismissed a report that alleged his administration pushed to include his name on Ford’s Theatre, calling it “a ridiculous lie.”

“The story that the White House, or me, want to affix my name to Ford’s Theatre, in Washington, D.C., where Abraham Lincoln was assassinated, is a ridiculous lie. It is FAKE NEWS,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “Who would possibly want a name on such a tragic place?”

“The Dumocrats suffer from serious Trump Derangement Syndrome. They are Degenerates and Losers who make up lie after lie, and this Ford’s Theatre Hoax is just another one of their never-ending, malicious falsehoods to try to discredit and demean,” he continued.

The MS NOW report stated that former and current White House officials told the outlet discussions had emerged about renaming the historical landmark, but it was unclear where the proposal stood. It further alleged that officials, advisers and allies close to Trump pitched adding his name to different sites and buildings in an effort to please the president.

Ford’s Theatre is designated a National Historical Site by the National Park Service (NPS) and is the site where President Abraham Lincoln was assassinated in 1865.

Trump added Thursday in a Truth Social post that it was “FAKE NEWS started by MSDNC AND CNN.”

The Trump administration has attempted to change Washington’s landmarks with several proposed, in-development or completed projects, including a triumphal arch, as well as changes to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and the Kennedy Center.

Earlier this month, a federal judge blocked an effort by the Kennedy Center’s board — who were all hand-picked by Trump — to add the president’s name to the institution and to rename its campus after Trump.

“If we’re going to save the Kennedy Center, I think the Trump administration should be given recognition for doing so,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office before the ruling.

The arch is also receiving criticism from veterans groups due to the arch’s location in the Memorial Circle; the 250-foot arch would break the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The project also would result in “ adverse effects ” to nearly 40 historical locations in Washington, according to an NPS assessment .

articles.title: Senate Republican: Iranian leaders ‘part of a colony of reptiles’ that also includes China, Russia, North Korea
articles.summary: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) on Wednesday accused Iran’s leaders of being “part of a colony of reptiles,” grouping them with other U.S. adversaries. Kennedy was responding to Fox News’s Will Cain on his eponymous show when asked about President Trump attending the United Nations General Assembly in New York City. Trump was part of a…
articles.body:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) on Wednesday accused Iran’s leaders of being “part of a colony of reptiles,” grouping them with other U.S. adversaries.

Kennedy was responding to Fox News’s Will Cain on his eponymous show when asked about President Trump attending the United Nations General Assembly in New York City.

Trump was part of a meeting with Iranian officials on the sidelines of the international body on Tuesday. The next day, he rolled out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews.

“I think that the people running Iran are reptiles,” Kennedy replied. “And they’re part of a colony of reptiles: China, North Korea, Russia and, as I said, Iran. The chief reptile, the quarterback, is President Xi in China. You can’t trust any of them.”

Kennedy said that in many ways, Iran, China, North Korea and Russia “are the same.”

“It’s like the same hooker in different dresses,” the Louisiana Republican continued. “They all lie like timeshare salesmen. You can’t trust them. I wouldn’t turn my back on any of them, even if I thought and knew they were two days dead.”

Kennedy defended the Trump administration’s military operation against Iran, reiterating the president’s frequent remark that the U.S. has “degraded Iran substantially” and that the country has “accomplished all of our goals.”

“They’re angry because President Trump has ripped Iran a new ashtray,” he said.

The senator insisted that China could open the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial passageway for roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil that Iran effectively shut off at the start of the conflict. Kennedy said the strait was the only problem remaining.

“And at some point, the president’s going to have to decide whether having achieved all of our objectives –– it’s time to come home and let China and Russia and North Korea and Europe and all the other countries that refuse to help take a crack at it because they’re going to pay the price of a closed strait even more than America,” he added.

Trump met with the Iranian delegation for three hours, with his son-in-law Jared Kushner in attendance. The president had earlier delivered a speech to the U.N. about his options in bringing the Iran war to a close: to seek a new deal on Iran’s nuclear program or allow the country to face “annihilation.”

On Wednesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the General Assembly that his country will not surrender or give up its nuclear program. He said Trump and others “who seek to bully us” must understand that Iran seeks a path toward peace “without accepting the language of force.”

“We will never bow our head or bend at the knee,” Pezeshkian said.

Xi’s visit to the U.S. marks the first official state visit from a Chinese leader in more than a decade as tensions between China and the U.S. remain high. He and Trump will hold a series of high-stakes meetings on Thursday before a state dinner at the White House. The two leaders are expected to talk about trade, artificial intelligence and the U.S. shipping weapons to Taiwan.

Both leaders agreed to ease tensions in their trade war last October, but neither made progress at their May summit in Beijing.

China hawks from both parties have expressed objections to Trump’s no-expense-spared treatment for Xi.

“Had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States, based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party,” Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said on the Senate floor Tuesday evening.

articles.title: When will America finally implement the 9/11 Commission’s security recommendations?
articles.summary: The government does not need another commission to identify weaknesses in border security. It just needs to finish the work already recommended.
articles.body:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the government still has not fully implemented important immigration-related recommendations in the 9/11 Commission Report .

Congress established the bipartisan commission in late 2002, to determine why we were vulnerable to the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and what could be done to prevent another attack from occurring. It released its report in 2004.

On Sept. 11, 2025, House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) and ranking member Jim Himes (D-Conn.) announced a bipartisan review of the recommendations made in the 9/11 Commission’s report, “to identify possible gaps or areas of improvement.” The committee conducted hearings and briefings both public and closed to gather the information it needed.

Nearly a year later, the committee issued its own report, which includes a roadmap for fully implementing the immigration-related recommendations of the 9/11 Commission.

1. Establish a higher bar for determining whether individuals are who they claim to be.

According to the 9/11 Commission, their “investigation showed that two systemic weaknesses came together in our border system’s inability to contribute to an effective defense against the 9/11 attacks: a lack of well-developed counterterrorism measures as a part of border security and an immigration system not able to deliver on its basic commitments, much less support counterterrorism.”

All 19 of the 9/11 hijackers entered the United States as nonimmigrant visitors — 18 on visitor visas for tourism or to conduct business and one on a student visa. The commission’s report observes that terrorists use evasive methods when they travel to avoid being detected, “such as altered and counterfeit passports and visas [and] specific travel methods and routes.” If the travel documents and travel patterns of the 9/11 hijackers had been examined more thoroughly, border officers might have found “as many of 15 of the 19 hijackers were potentially vulnerable to interception by border authorities.”

Moreover, it wasn’t necessary to recognize that they were inadmissible as terrorists . With exceptions that are not relevant here, an alien is presumed to be an immigrant until he establishes that he is entitled to a claimed nonimmigrant status. It would have been sufficient, therefore, just to determine that the attackers had failed to establish they were entitled to the nonimmigrant classifications they claimed.

2. Finish the biometric entry-exit system.

The 9/11 Commission recommended establishing a biometric entry-exit system as quickly as possible following the attacks. Biometrics are defined by the Department of Homeland Security as the automated identification of individuals “based on their biological and behavioral characteristics from which distinguishing, repeatable biometric features can be extracted for the purpose of biometric recognition.” Such characteristics include fingerprints, iris patterns and facial features.

Homeland Security already provides the technology needed for a biometric entry-exit system to store, compare and share biometric data through its Office of Biometric Identity Management . But despite the efforts of the executive branch and Congress, our biometric entry-exit system still has not been fully implemented.

The 2025 committee’s report states that air, sea and pedestrian points of entry all have fully implemented systems for entry biometrics. Challenges remain, however, with collecting biometrics on aliens entering in vehicles, and exit biometric systems have not been fully implemented yet either. However, new technology such as artificial intelligence improvements in facial recognition makes it possible to achieve more today than was possible when the 9/11 Commission made this recommendation.

It should be noted, however, that while exit data tells the government which nonimmigrant visitors have overstayed their admission period, it has limited enforcement value unless Immigration and Customs Enforcement can determine where they are.

3. Make immigration, law enforcement and intelligence databases interoperable.

The 9/11 Commission recommended improvements in information sharing between intelligence agencies and with federal agencies beyond the intelligence community. It suggested establishing a “decentralized network model” that would permit officers across agencies to access one another’s reports, with appropriate security measures for classified information.

The committee’s report today states that great progress has been made in information sharing within the intelligence community, but that improvement is needed between intelligence and law enforcement agencies and with federal agencies outside of the intelligence community.

4. Use task-force partnerships for immigration-related national security cases.

The 9/11 Commission observed that unvetted travelers pose a serious threat to national security. It recommended closer interaction between the intelligence community and border security agencies.

The House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence recommends mission-centered interagency task forces rather than agency-owned programs. This would facilitate cooperation between the agencies.

The government does not need another commission to identify weaknesses in border security. It just needs to finish the work already recommended.

Nolan Rappaport was detailed to the House Judiciary Committee as an executive branch immigration law expert for three years. He subsequently served as an immigration counsel for the Subcommittee on Immigration, Border Security and Claims for four years. Prior to working on the Judiciary Committee, he wrote decisions for the Board of Immigration Appeals for 20 years. Follow his blog at

articles.title: Obama: Government is ‘so much less corrupt than probably it’s ever been’
articles.summary: Former President Obama says in his just-launched literary-focused podcast that the federal government is “so much less corrupt” than it was in the past. “People are always surprised when I tell them the federal government is so much less corrupt than probably it’s ever been, in terms of just pure bribes, or patronage or favors,” Obama said…
articles.body:
Former President Obama says in his just-launched literary-focused podcast that the federal government is “so much less corrupt” than it was in the past.

“People are always surprised when I tell them the federal government is so much less corrupt than probably it’s ever been, in terms of just pure bribes, or patronage or favors,” Obama said in a preview clip exclusively obtained by ITK from the 44th president’s new podcast, “A Great Book with Barack Obama.”

The six-episode series — in which Obama sits down with high-profile figures to chat about the “books that have profoundly shaped his worldview and our society” — premiered on Audible on Thursday.

In the third episode of the limited series, produced by Audible and the Obamas’ production company, Higher Ground, the ex-commander in chief sits down with Pulitzer Prize-winning historian Jill Lepore to discuss Robert Penn Warren’s 1946 novel “All the King’s Men.”

“It was interesting, as I was coming up through the state legislature, and then Congress and the presidency — you mentioned Lyndon Johnson, part of the reason that kind of cornering folks and hustling them for votes worked, it wasn’t just physical intimidation. It was like, ‘What do you need?'” Obama told Lepore while discussing the book about a fictional farmer-turned-populist governor’s rise and eventual downfall amid political corruption in the South.

“Part of what was interesting is that a lot of reforms that we think of as positive — pre-Watergate, post-Watergate — eliminated or greatly reduced the possibilities of maintaining those old political machines, and trading votes and doing favors,” Obama, 65, said.

“And it’s part of the reason why things got a little harder to get done because that was sort of some lubrication in a lot of Congress to help to bridge some of the ideological differences that were out there and get people to vote for things that weren’t that comfortable,” he said.

Saying she agreed with Obama, Lepore replied, “I think there’s a degree to which that kind of political machine — I don’t mean to whitewash it in any way — but was kind of crucial to civil society.”

“Like what happened in the Progressive Era, among the many good government reforms that these people were making — campaign finance reform and protections for voters — yeah, it did kill the political machine. But what replaced the political machine was the political consultants industry,” Lepore, a staff writer for The New Yorker, said.

Other episodes of Obama’s podcast include conversations with actor Tom Hanks about “Gilead,” by Marilynne Robinson; a discussion of James Baldwin’s “The Fire Next Time” with author and journalist Ta-Nehisi Coates; and chats with former White House national security adviser Ben Rhodes and authors Percival Everett and Lauren Groff.

articles.body:
Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) said Wednesday she is not as concerned over democratic socialists potentially entering the House than she is with Republican lawmakers she deemed “complicit” with President Trump.

“I am far less worried about some person who espouses some DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] title winning and coming into our caucus than I’m worried about those who are in the Republican caucus, who are complicit with the president,” she told host Chris Cuomo on NewsNation’s “Cuomo.”

A string of democratic socialists won primaries this year in solidly blue districts, including Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Melat Kiros in Colorado and Donavan McKinney in Michigan, along with Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York City .

Three of those candidates knocked off incumbent House Democrats, capitalizing on voters’ frustrations with the economy .

Trump and GOP lawmakers have argued the left-wing victories indicate “communists” have overtaken the Democratic Party, despite none of them being associated with the ideology. During the Republican Party’s midterm convention earlier this month, the president reiterated his stance .

“You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell,” Trump told attendees. “You know that, OK? You go to hell, and I don’t want that to happen to you. So please go and vote, because together we will defeat the communists.”

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) also said at the convention Democrats are mired in their own “Bolshevik Revolution” and will “raise taxes on every hardworking American” if they reclaim control of Congress.

As of Wednesday, Decision Desk HQ gave Democrats a 52 percent chance of taking back the Senate and House in November. The latest generic congressional ballot from Emerson College Polling also has Democrats leading Republicans 53 percent to 42 percent.

Democratic candidates in red states have recently pushed back on the GOP attack line. Kansas Senate candidate Adam Hamilton (D) said in a recent ad that “both extremes just don’t get it,” criticizing the left and his opponent , Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.).

“On one side, the far left pushes socialism and open borders,” Hamilton said in the ad. “On the other side, Roger Marshall gives us higher gas and grocery prices while slashing our healthcare. What’s going on in Washington? It’s just not who we are.”

articles.body:
Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) on Wednesday criticized President Trump’s decision to greet Chinese President Xi Jinping with fanfare during the leader’s arrival at Joint Base Andrews.

“This is actually pretty consistent for Trump,” the senator told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins. “He loves dictators, and he loves the power that Xi Jinping represents, and I think this is the president really saying to the leader of China, ‘Don’t hurt me.’”

Xi is visiting the U.S. for a three-day state visit that has drawn criticism from Democrats and some Republican lawmakers.

In a Senate floor speech on Tuesday, Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) said he would have advised the president to “not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome.”

On Wednesday, the president and first lady Melania Trump greeted Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the end of a 100-foot red carpet. The welcome ceremony included a cannon salute, a 21-person honor cordon and color guards displaying the U.S. and Chinese flags.

The visit follows a bilateral summit between the two leaders in Beijing earlier this year, where Trump was greeted by Xi upon arrival at the Great Hall of the People with a military welcome and groups of schoolchildren holding flowers and waving flags.

During Xi’s visit to the nation’s capital, the leaders are expected to discuss trade and the rapidly evolving artificial intelligence industry.

Warren, who has called for a pause on advanced development amid concerns about the dangers of the technology, urged the president to cut off the sale of critical AI chip technology to China.

“That’s where the president should start,” she told Collins on Wednesday.

“And then, having made clear that we’re going to cut off that supply for China, we should sit down and start negotiating with China for better constraints on AI overall to make sure we are keeping our people safe, that we are keeping the world safe,” the Massachusetts Democrat added.

Trump, who has repeatedly brushed aside rising concerns about the potential dangers of AI, said Thursday that the technology “will be a big topic of discussion” during his meeting with Xi.

“I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also,” he wrote on Truth Social , adding that the Justice Department is “our guardrail.”

articles.title: Top public university’s ‘LGBTQ+ lab’ hit with race-bias complaint amid $700K in Trump-era federal funding
articles.summary: The University of Maryland's Lavender Lab faces a Title VI complaint alleging its advisory board and hiring practices discriminate based on race.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A University of Maryland research lab that received nearly $700,000 in additional federal funding from the Trump administration this year is facing a civil rights complaint alleging that it uses race and ethnicity to determine access to some research-related opportunities. The Equal Protection Project (EPP) filed the complaint with the Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights against UMD's Lavender Lab, a National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded lab that studies suicide, substance use and other health outcomes among LGBTQ+ people and Black, Indigenous and People of Color. EPP is asking HHS to investigate whether the lab's LGBTQ+ Teens of Color Advisory Board and its research assistant selection practices give priority to non-White applicants. "Some people may ask what is wrong with prioritizing non-whites in a program which is designed to study non-whites," EPP founder William Jacobson told Fox News Digital. "When you receive federal funding, you cannot discriminate in the administration of your programs." JUSTICE DEPARTMENT LAUNCHES TITLE VI INVESTIGATION INTO DEI PROGRAMS AT ARIZONA STATE UNIVERSITY "You do not need to have an advisory board, you do not need to hire research assistants based on race to fulfill the purposes of this grant," Jacobson continued. The complaint comes as the Lavender Lab continues receiving millions of dollars through the NIH for research examining alcohol and drug use among "sexual minority adolescents of color." One of the lab's principal projects, titled "Long-Term and Daily Associations Among Intersectional Minority Stress, Structural Oppression, and Alcohol Use and Misuse Among Sexual Minority Adolescents of Color," began in May 2022 and is scheduled to run through April 2027. The complaint cites approximately $3.6 million in total federal obligations and roughly $2.2 million in outlays at the time of its filing. NIH records cited in the complaint show the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism provided another $695,192 for the project for fiscal year 2026. The complaint points first to the lab's LGBTQ+ Teens of Color Advisory Board, which said it was "specifically looking for teens in the US who identify as both LGBTQ+ and Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC) to join our board" in an Instagram post. A NEW YORK UNIVERSITY FACES JUSTICE DEPARTMENT INVESTIGATION OVER 'BLACK MALE INITIATIVE' According to the complaint, board members are paid to help review research, provide feedback and participate in professional-development activities, with some also receiving leadership opportunities. EPP also targeted the Lavender Lab's research-assistant program, which offers positions to undergraduate and master's-level students. Although the positions are generally unpaid, the complaint stated that undergraduate research assistants may receive academic course credit, and some students may be able to participate through federal work-study. Research assistants generally commit to at least two semesters and a minimum of eight hours per week. The lab stated it "especially encourage[s] and invite[s] candidates from traditionally marginalized backgrounds" to apply and that applicants with experience conducting research involving "LGBTQ and BIPOC communities" through "cultural humility, intersectionality, and social justice approaches" will receive the "strongest consideration." "Discrimination based on race or ethnicity at institutions receiving federal funding is unlawful regardless of which group is targeted or benefits," Jacobson said. "Treating individuals as avatars of their demographic identity rather than as individuals with unique merits and circumstances undermines fairness, merit, social cohesion, and the rule of law." TRUMP ADMIN'S PUSH TO SCRAP DEI IN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT TAKES LANDMARK STEP WITH NEW HIRING RULE EPP alleges that the language indicates race or ethnicity may play a role in the selection process. The complaint asks HHS to investigate whether the practices violate Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in federally funded programs, as well as the Affordable Care Act. "Because the Lavender Lab is operating under an HHS health care related grant, the non-discrimination provisions of the Affordable Care Act must be adhered to, and HHS has authority to enforce those provisions," Jacobson said. EPP's complaint also questions federal funding for research focused on intersectionality, which the Lavender Lab says guides its work. The lab studies how sexual-minority status, race, ethnicity and what it calls "structural oppression" affect health outcomes. "The conduct at the Lavender Lab calls into question whether HHS should be funding intersectionality-focused research at all," Jacobson said. "Intersectionality is a race- and ethnicity-focused group-identity approach. It is no surprise that where the focus is racial identity that programming could cross the line into civil rights violations." Jacobson said EPP has found federal dollars going to programs that use intersectionality and is calling for tighter rules on that funding. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "We have identified hundreds of millions of dollars of federal funding for programs that incorporate intersectionality," Jacobson said. "Given the civil rights danger from an 'intersectional' approach, we call on the administration to issue a new executive order and agency guidance closing the 'intersectionality loophole' by including intersectionality in the ban on unlawful discriminatory DEI practices in federal grantmaking." articles.title: Trump media ban: White House restores access to CNN, Politico and MS NOW after judge's order
articles.summary: CNN, Politico and MS NOW were allowed back into the White House after some of their staff were earlier turned away.
articles.body:
CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters have been allowed back into the White House after they sought an emergency court hearing to restore their revoked press access.

They accused the White House in a court filing of having "repeatedly violated" a judge's order lifting President Donald Trump's ban on the three media outlets.

But the White House said in a filing that it began reinstating access shortly after 09:00 EDT (13:00 GMT) on Thursday.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico reported they were granted entry hours after some of their staff were turned away. Trump initially said he barred the outlets because of "fake news". The White House later cited national security.

In the early hours, Judge Timothy Kelly had ruled the ban on the outlets should be temporarily lifted because it "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".

The White House in its filing said that the press passes had been restored by 09:07 local time and that confiscated badges were available starting at 09:45.

The standoff limited some TV coverage as Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House ahead of a state dinner.

CNN said some of their journalists were denied entry, including senior White House reporter Betsy Klein. But a producer was allowed to enter, the outlet reported.

Politico said one of its reporters was denied access to the White House and had his press credentials confiscated.

MS NOW reported that its White House reporter Laura Barrón-López and a producer were barred and had their passes taken, but another MS NOW producer was allowed in.

Trump first announced last Friday he was barring CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.

By Saturday morning, each outlet reported that they were denied entry to the White House grounds and that their press badges were confiscated.

All three outlets spoke out against the ban, accusing the Trump administration of violating their constitutional rights.

In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports".

TV networks including Fox News, NBC, CBS and ABC had suspended their televised coverage of the White House in solidarity.

And more than 50 media organisations across the ideological spectrum filed an amicus brief in support of the lawsuit, including Fox News, the New York Times, the Washington Post and the Wall Street Journal.

There have been previous instances of administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.

The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a specific press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.

But after objections from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was allowed in.

articles.title: Attacks and threats against federal judges have spiked, and it threatens our democracy
articles.summary: If those in power continue attacking judges with violent words and images without consequence, we risk losing the founders’ design of judicial independence.
articles.body:
In the 10 years since I left my position as a federal district judge in the Southern District of New York, there has been an unprecedented spike in the threats and harassment targeting federal judges throughout the country.

I know from personal experience what it means to be the subject of violent threats just for doing my job. After one ruling, the U.S. Marshals began driving me to work. After another ruling, the press screamed that it would be my fault if New York City blew up due to a rise in crime.

But the environment surrounding attacks on judges is now far worse. The frequency and volume of harassment are at extreme levels. Judges I know are committed to upholding the rule of law despite these conditions, but they deserve better protection. They also deserve more respect from politicians, pundits and influencers, who have turned disagreement with a ruling into a barrage of violent rhetoric aimed squarely at the judges and their families.

In a recent Brennan Center for Justice report , 35 sitting and retired federal judges, myself included, spoke about their experiences with violent threats.

Take one striking example: After ruling against the Trump administration in a case related to immigration enforcement, a federal district judge received more than 700 threatening phone calls in chambers. The harassment went beyond the courthouse. The judge’s personal information was circulated online, including the floor plan of this judge’s home. The threats became serious enough that the judge’s family spent significant personal funds to strengthen home security, and their child’s school was compelled to increase the number of active shooter training sessions.

District judges appointed by both Democratic and Republican presidents have been on the front lines in upholding the rule of law, including halting illegal assertions of power by the president. Judges have seen their families threatened and lives upended for carrying out their constitutional responsibilities. Some have required protective details around the clock. According to data provided by the judiciary , “security incidents of significant concern” for judges increased by 57 percent in the 2025 fiscal year and are on pace to rise again this year.

Threats can turn to tragedy. Judge Esther Salas of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey paid a high price for her work as a judge: In 2020, her family was targeted in a deadly attack that left her husband severely injured and her only son murdered.

Yet in the face of intimidation, federal district judges across the country, and coming from a wide array of judicial philosophies, continue to stand their ground, issuing rulings based solely on the law and the facts. I am proud of them and of our profession.

As any judge will tell you, fierce criticism is part of the job. During my tenure, I heard a case involving a Jordanian student named Osama Awadallah who was charged with making false statements before a grand jury investigating the 9/11 attacks on the World Trade Center.

When a jury acquitted Awadallah of all the charges, news headlines called me “ Osama’s Favorite Judge ,” playing off the defendant’s shared name with Osama bin Laden. My chambers received letters saying I should have died in the Twin Towers. Other colleagues hearing high-profile cases required full-time security details.

But as the Brennan Center report details, today’s threat landscape for judges is unprecedented. What once might have generated an angry letter can now become a social media post that goes viral and generates hundreds of threats. Judges’ addresses and other personal information are often easily found online.

Political leaders have often added fuel to the fire with inflammatory and irresponsible rhetoric, with then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche saying the administration was at “war” with “rogue” judges, and Trump calling judges “ lunatics ” and “ monsters .”

One judge’s name and face was posted on a “wanted” poster in the halls of Congress . He was also “swatted” — someone called the police anonymously claiming the judge had barricaded himself in his house and murdered his wife to generate an armed response — and he received a fake pipe bomb threat in his mailbox.

If those in power continue attacking judges with violent words and images without consequence, we risk losing the founders’ design of judicial independence that once made our democracy the envy of the civilized world.

The courts should be the place where disputes are resolved peacefully — where the law rather than intimidation determines the outcome. If mounting threats and baseless impeachments influence who is willing to serve as a judge, how judges make decisions or whether their families can live safely, we risk allowing intimidation to infect the judicial process.

That is a price no democracy can afford.

Shira A. Scheindlin is a former judge of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.

articles.title: Female athletes, women's sports advocates speak on Capitol Hill as trans athlete issue hovers over midterms
articles.summary: Female athletes descended on Capitol Hill Wednesday to testify how biological males in women's sports threatened their safety and locker room privacy.
articles.body: Female athletes and women’s sports advocates descended on Capitol Hill Wednesday to tell lawmakers how policies allowing biological males to compete in female athletics have affected their safety, privacy and athletic opportunities, while warning that the issue could follow candidates into the midterm elections. The Senate Judiciary Committee held a hearing titled, "Standing Up for Women in Sports: Ensuring Opportunity, Fairness and Safety for Female Athletes." The committee heard testimony from three witnesses: Independent Council on Women’s Sports (ICONS) co-founder Kim Jones; Carly Smolak, a former professional soccer player and Australian rules football player; and attorney William Bock III, who previously served as general counsel for the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency. Democrats did not invite a witness of their own. Ranking member Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., were the only Democrats who attended, and both left within the first hour. Durbin declined to question the witnesses. Jones, whose daughter competed against transgender swimmer Lia Thomas, told OutKick in an exclusive interview that the Democrats’ absence made the athletes and advocates feel dismissed. AMERICANS CLASH OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES AS DEBATE HEATS UP: ‘JUST GETTING OUTRAGEOUS' "It felt dismissive of women, of our concerns, of the right for young girls to expect to be treated fairly in the United States," Jones said. "For Democrats to say that we’re — I believe, you know, are my neighbors and friends — to actively say we’re not going to concern ourselves about what young girls and even all the way up through older women have been put through. "I mean, it’s misogynistic, and it is incredibly disappointing. I really hope that they change course and decide that the voices of women who have been hurt and shamed are important enough to listen to." Durbin used his opening remarks to argue that the hearing was ignoring other issues facing children and female athletes, including affordability, artificial intelligence, children’s cellphone use and declining trust in government. He also raised concerns that efforts to enforce sex-based sports categories could result in female athletes undergoing invasive inspections. Jones rejected both arguments. "It was incensing," she said of Durbin’s remarks. "One of the worst comments you can give to women who are trying to share the stories of what they’ve been put through by the denial of their sex and the denial of their rights is to suggest that this is not an important issue and that it’s dismissible. "It’s akin to saying, ‘I cannot care about brain cancer until you solve stomach cancer.’ It’s whataboutism in the most obvious form and telling women that we are not going to address the problems that you’re facing, including sexual abuse and harassment by the inclusion of male athletes in women’s sports and women’s locker rooms, until we solve every other problem in the world." OLYMPIC SWIMMER RÉKA GYÖRGY CALLS OUT VIRGINIA GOVERNOR SPANBERGER FOR WITHDRAWING FEMALE SPORTS REGULATION Jones said sex eligibility could be determined without invasive examinations, pointing to cheek-swab testing for the SRY gene. "There is no need for any kind of invasive inspections. There’s no need for any kind of traumatic experience," Jones said. Asked whether she expects the issue to influence the midterms, Jones said the protection of female sports should be "non-negotiable." "Of course," Jones said. "I think truth is always an important issue for anyone voting in the general public. I think that standing up for the rights and fair treatment of women in the United States is a ground-zero, non-negotiable issue. And this is a blatant public display of stripping that from women and girls." Smolak testified about discovering that a registered sex offender had joined an adult women’s Australian rules football team with which she remained closely connected after retiring. She said the individual was quietly removed after she raised the issue, but alleged that team members were not informed and the sport’s national governing body did not take sufficient action to prevent a similar situation. "So it felt like at every single level, the national level and largely the media level, it feels like nobody was doing anything about this issue," Smolak told OutKick exclusively. "And I didn’t want to see this happen again. If it happened once, it’ll happen again if we don’t put policies in place. And the obvious policy is that women’s sports are for biological females, are for women." SPANBERGER SPARKS OUTRAGE AFTER SNEAKILY ENDING YOUNGKIN-ERA WOMEN'S SPORTS PROTECTIONS Smolak said the response she encountered after raising concerns was "incredibly disheartening." "I’ve had people be more concerned about using his preferred pronouns than trying to prevent this from happening again or being even upset that it happened in the first place," she said. Smolak said she was not surprised Democratic senators did not remain to hear the full testimony. "I think they either know they have a losing issue or cannot make their argument based on the merits of their position," Smolak said. "And so they would rather distract about other issues that are unrelated or just not show up at all. But it’s infuriating." Following the hearing, additional female athletes spoke at a Capitol Hill press conference. Briley Lechner, a 17-year-old varsity volleyball and soccer player at Monroe High School in New York, said she and her teammates learned only after a volleyball match that a biological male had competed against them and entered their locker room. "All of us girls do our normal things. We get undressed, unconsciously trusting our friends next to us. We have girl conversations. We take girl pictures, videos and everything like that," Lechner said. "So to be told days after that there was a boy in the locker room where we get undressed, and there was a boy on the other side of the court, just is very hurtful. And it feels as if our protection was just stripped away from us and they don’t care." Lechner said the backlash she and her father received after speaking publicly would not silence her. "I’m not going to sit down until there is a change," she said. "And I’m going to continue to speak my word and share my story until us girls don’t have to feel uncomfortable and we don’t have to be fearful — not only in the locker room, but in the bathroom, on the court, on the field and any other sport." Former West Virginia State University soccer player Lainey Armistead discussed her involvement in litigation over West Virginia’s law restricting girls’ and women’s sports to biological females. The Supreme Court upheld West Virginia’s law earlier this year. "There are still girls in 23 other states, girls in New York, girls in California, who do not have the same opportunities that I did," Armistead said. "And we will not quit fighting for those girls. Women’s sports is not men’s for the taking." NCAA softball player Kendall Kotzmacher said her high school team lost in a state semifinal to a team with a transgender pitcher during her senior year. "Showing up to the field that day knowing that we were playing a man is a feeling that you can’t explain to another person," Kotzmacher said. "Showing up, seeing a male on the field for something you’ve worked your whole life for, and knowing there’s nothing you can do about it is unimaginable." Kotzmacher directly addressed Democrats who have minimized the prevalence of such cases. "To the Democrats that said this is a non-issue, they’re the reason that I’m going to keep speaking out and everyone else is going to keep speaking out," she said. "We have multiple women here that have suffered the same things that I have. And there are so many more that have stayed silent because people out there have told them not to speak up, who have scared them into not speaking up." U.S. Masters swimmer Angie Griffin said she lost a national title to a transgender competitor at the 2025 U.S. Masters Swimming Spring National Championship. Griffin said a grievance alleging unsportsmanlike conduct was filed against her after she and other swimmers protested the results, exposing her to a potential lifetime ban before she was cleared. "The process itself was the punishment," Griffin said. "The message to other women was clear: Speak up and you will pay a price." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "Women should not have to lose a championship, risk a ban, hire a lawyer or face public pressure simply to ask for a fair race," she added. "The path forward is clear: Prioritize women in women’s sports." Marshi Smith, a former NCAA champion swimmer and fellow ICONS co-founder, said the athletes’ accounts showed why adults in leadership positions needed to intervene. "It was a historic moment to see this issue come to such a huge platform, but it was also incredibly distressing to see that the Democrat senators were so dismissive of young women who are suffering across the country today," Smith said. "There are huge threats to women’s sports today, and adults really need to stand up in leadership positions and do something about it." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! OutKick contacted all 10 Democratic committee members about their absences. Only Durbin’s office responded, pointing to his opening statement. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., later told OutKick that he missed the hearing because of a classified briefing on the Iran war, but declined to discuss his position on women’s sports. Kotzmacher said the absence and dismissal of the issue only strengthened her resolve. "So to the Democrats, we’re going to keep speaking up. We’re going to keep fighting for women, and we’re not going to stop."

articles.title: Peltola campaign rips New York Times report on tumultuous operations
articles.summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-Alaska) Senate campaign has pushed back against a report from The New York Times on Wednesday that detailed chaos in her campaign operation. Several former Peltola aides who requested anonymity told the Times about profane outbursts and displays of anger throughout the campaign and her former congressional office. The tensions also…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-Alaska) Senate campaign has pushed back against a report from The New York Times on Wednesday that detailed chaos in her campaign operation.

Several former Peltola aides who requested anonymity told the Times about profane outbursts and displays of anger throughout the campaign and her former congressional office. The tensions also allegedly led to a staffing shakeup days before Alaska’s August primary.

Her campaign denied any pattern of problematic behavior, but it acknowledged she “sometimes struggled to deal with her grief” after the 2023 deaths of her mother and husband. Eugene Peltola was killed in a plane crash .

“At the time of their passing, Mary was parenting kids through their own grief, serving full-time in the U.S. House of Representatives thousands of miles from home, and running a competitive re-election campaign — all while shouldering the enormous burden of grief,” Peltola spokesperson Harry Child said in a statement shared with The Hill.

“But she treats her staff with respect and care, and she maintains close positive relationships with her staff spanning her nearly 30 years in public service. Exaggerating and outright lying about moments from the hardest period of her life, and falsely presenting them as a pattern of behavior, is wrong,” Child said.

Peltola declined to answer reporters’ questions about the allegations in the report at a Wednesday town hall, according to Alaska News Source.

The report details one early 2024 incident in which Peltola, frustrated about not finding a memo, allegedly shoved a male employee in the chest, which the campaign described as an accidental bump. In a 2024 text reviewed by The Times, the congresswoman wrote “f‑‑‑ those b‑‑‑‑es” amid frustrations with Planned Parenthood. At the time, Peltola was running for reelection to the House.

The campaign acknowledged to the Times that Peltola had used an ableist slur and regretted doing so, and it denied allegations that she had used a homophobic slur.

Other staffers described tumult over Peltola’s daughter’s pet chameleon, Meatball, whose diet of live crickets escaped in her Capitol Hill office on at least one occasion. Still, more friends and former aides shared only positive experiences with the Times.

The Times also reported that Peltola, frustrated with her staff, brought in a new consultant ahead of this year’s primary. After some staffers told the consultant they intended to quit, the report alleges, the campaign fired longtime manager Elisa Rios and demoted chief of staff Anton McParland.

Peltola, who lost Alaska’s at-large House seat to Republican Rep. Nick Begich in 2024, is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan for the Senate seat this fall. Her moderate, Alaska-first bid has fueled Democrats’ hopes of flipping the seat in the Last Frontier, which has sided with President Trump in each of his three presidential races.

Alaska has elected a Democrat to the Senate just once in the past 50 years, but Cook Political Report rates this year’s race as a toss-up. Decision Desk HQ gives Peltola an even better chance, rating it as “lean Democratic.”

articles.title: American businesses aren’t allowed to build. It’s time Congress helped them
articles.summary: Permitting delays average over two years and cost millions, crushing small manufacturers and defense startups before they can begin production.
articles.body: America’s share of global manufacturing output has fallen from 25% in 1997 to 15% today. Absent intervention, it could reach 11% by 2030. Those numbers get thrown around a lot. What is said less is what they mean for Americans: The United States is losing its ability to produce the things it needs to defend itself, to power its economy and to care for its people. This failure is not because we lack talent, capital or technology. It is because we have made it nearly impossible to build anything here. This inability to build harms every American industry and every American job. Whether it is semiconductor fabricators, munitions or battery factories, rare earth production facilities, natural gas pipelines, oil refineries or medical manufacturing centers, all hit the same regulatory barrier: federal permitting law. INNOVATION IS KEY TO AMERICA STAYING A SUPERPOWER. BUT IT IS MISSING AN ESSENTIAL PIECE Among the various federal permitting barriers, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) stands as the most egregious. Unlike substantive environmental protections found in statutes like the Clean Water Act and the Clean Air Act, NEPA’s central function is procedural, requiring analysis and disclosure of environmental impacts before major federal actions. Over time, regulatory layering and aggressive legal interpretation transformed this reasonable "look before you leap" statute into a roadblock for projects with any sort of federal connection. SENATE REPUBLICAN PUSHES OVERHAUL TO CUT RED TAPE AND SPEED UP AMERICAN ENERGY PROJECTS This regulatory accretion has turned NEPA into a tool to stop nearly any meaningful project — across every state and political spectrum. It is not every day renewable energy advocates and oil and gas executives work together to reform a statute. Yet these and many other strange bedfellows have come together this year to fix a profoundly broken statute and allow America to build again. The numbers explain why. The median NEPA review in 2024 ran 26 months. The statute’s more demanding environmental impact statements averaged 3.8 years. Environmental assessments, the so-called fast track, routinely average a year or more. None of those timelines are legally required. They are what happens when bureaucratic caution and unlimited litigation combine in the absence of any countervailing pressure. TRUMP-APPROVED ENERGY PROJECTS AT RISK OF SUDDEN DEATH BY NEXT HOSTILE PRESIDENT And then there is the cost. DOE data showed mean environmental assessment preparation costs were over $300,000 while environmental impact statement costs averaged $6.6 million. Those figures exclude legal fees, staff time and the cost of litigation. These millions add to the bottom line of every potential domestic manufacturing project. For a major company, these delays and costs are annoying. For a small business seeking to open a factory or a startup raising its first manufacturing round, they are often a company-ending event. AMERICA FACES A CRISIS IN OUR MILITARY ARSENAL THAT TRUMP IS RACING TO FIX These are the types of businesses America most needs right now–the 50-person drone manufacturer, the battery startup and the defense tech company that won a Pentagon contract and needs to be in production before its runway expires are exactly the companies the current NEPA regime destroys. These are also the jobs Americans need. This regulatory Sisyphean task doesn’t improve outcomes, it materially delays or even kills meritorious projects. Investors cannot deploy capital if regulatory uncertainty clouds a project. SEN KEVIN CRAMER: CHINA BUILDS FOR WAR WHILE AMERICA WAITS ON PERMITS While the Supreme Court’s "Seven County" decision and recent executive actions have helped, only Congress can enact durable statutory reforms needed to restore NEPA to its intended procedural role. Here are some basic fixes. Over time, regulatory layering and aggressive legal interpretation transformed this reasonable "look before you leap" statute into a roadblock for projects with any sort of federal connection. Enforce the deadlines and limit endless litigation TRUMP ADMIN MOVES TO GUT BIDEN'S SIGNATURE ENVIRONMENTAL RULES Agencies need to enforce permitting deadlines. Aspirational goals do not motivate federal bureaucrats, but neither does the prospect of getting dragged into court. Both extremes perpetuate analysis paralysis. Get the permits done and when they’re complete, there should be finality, providing certainty for manufacturers, the capital backing them and the federal agency granting the permit. Revocations should be permitted only when there is an imminent, irreparable and specifically documented harm. Cut the red tape for companies which can least afford it THE MACHINES THAT KEEP AMERICA ALIVE ARE FAILING. WE FORGOT HOW TO REPLACE THEM Agencies which finance or permit manufacturing already have categorical exclusions, pre-cleared categories of routine actions normally not requiring a full Environmental Assessment or Environmental Impact Statement. Most have never shared those categories with each other, despite a 2023 law explicitly allowing them to do so. Congress should require agencies that finance or permit manufacturing to adopt a curated list of relevant categorical exclusions from other agencies. This one reform alone would dramatically increase regulatory speed and certainty. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION None of this dismantles environmental protection. Clean air, clean water and endangered species protections all remain fully intact. What these reforms remove is the accumulated procedural weight which has nothing to do with those protections and everything to do with a system no one has been accountable for fixing. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The opportunity to build in America is now. Nobody left, right or center wants this to be an era of managed decline. We want growth, security and innovation. That is why political polar opposites are making great strides to reach a deal, like Chairmen Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.V., Environment and Public Works, and Mike Lee, R-Ut., Energy and Natural Resources, and Ranking Members Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Environment and Public Works, and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., Energy and Natural Resources . The American people will benefit from the good jobs and the supply security these reforms create. It’s time to meet the moment and get America building again. Katherine Boyle is a general partner at Andreessen Horowitz and co-lead of its American Dynamism practice. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM SEN. KEVIN CRAMER

articles.body:
Republican Rep. Byron Donalds (Fla.), who is running for governor in his state, said President Trump’s agenda is “common sense” following the removal of some mentions of the president’s name from Donalds’s campaign website.

CBS News reported that Donalds, in an interview at a local summit Wednesday, was pressed on the edits.

The Florida Republican said Trump’s agenda is a “commonsense agenda,” adding that it is “centered around law and order, sound markets, making sure that we secure our nation’s borders, making sure that we continue to work with the federal government when it comes to immigration policy,” according to the outlet.

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) recently shifted the Florida governor’s race to a toss-up amid a rough electoral environment for Republicans as they head into the midterms.

The apparent tightening of the race for Florida’s top job in a state that Trump has won in the last three elections may be a warning sign for Republicans as the midterms approach.

The old layout of Donalds’s website featured a banner at the top of the webpage that read “Chip in to Support Trump Endorsed Byron Donalds” and text below it that said “TRUMP-ENDORSED.”

Another bar that noted the endorsement next to a photo of Trump could be seen lower on the page.

Donalds’s newer layout only showed Trump’s endorsement in a box next to others for the Florida representative.

articles.title: Democrats hit Republicans with do-nothing charges after abrupt House adjournment
articles.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson abruptly ended the House of Representatives’ legislative session early to allow members to campaign for the upcoming midterm elections following several contentious votes on sanctions, impeachment resolutions, and a war powers measure.
articles.body:
Last week, the House of Representatives appeared to be suffering from nervous seat syndrome. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) had already cancelled the final two weeks of the pre-midterm election session. Then, late Wednesday, he abruptly canceled Thursday’s final day of legislative business , sending members home early to campaign. The Senate opted to remain in session through next week. Both chambers will return the second week in November.

The easy explanation for the House’s early exit is that with polls showing Republicans possibly losing House control in November, they need all the time they can get to rally their supporters to turn out at the polls. Representatives may have fewer accomplishments to justify their return to power, but that would not likely be remedied by two more frantic weeks of procedural wrangling.

It’s difficult to gin-up campaign issues to run on when polling shows that the party now controlling both branches is under water on most issues: from affordability and the Iran war, to corruption and AI. The fallback position seems to be, when in doubt, punt and run for home, i.e., your House seat.

The only major bill the House dealt with last week was on Wednesday when it agreed to the Senate amendments to the House-passed, Lindsey O. Graham Russian and Iran Sanctions Act , by a 262-159 vote . The president signed it into law on Friday .

On Tuesday, Sept. 15, Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) called up another of his joint resolutions to impeach President Donald Trump. Green has been a very vocal critic of the president, having been escorted off the floor the past two years for shouting at the president during his State of the Union Address. Green lost his Democratic run-off election this year due to Texas redistricting. The House tabled Green’s resolution 232-147 , without debate. Republicans voted 213-0 for tabling , while Democrats voted 18-147 against, with 46 Democrats voting “present.”

The second unscheduled privileged matter called up last Tuesday was a war powers resolution introduced by Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.). Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast (R-Fla.) offered a motion to discharge the resolution from his committee, subject to one-hour of debate. The resolution directed the president to withdraw U.S. armed forces from Iran, but exempted U.S. bases in the region from the withdrawal directive. It was the third time the House adopted an Iran withdrawal measure, this time approving it, 220-204 , with seven Republicans voting in favor — the greatest number of Republican members yet.

The final turn of the screw also occurred on Tuesday when Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) noticed his intention to call-up a resolution “ impeaching Peter Brian Hegseth, Secretary of Defense, for high crimes and misdemeanors .” The Speaker informally termed Massie’s resolution “a stunt,” but announced formally that, under the rules, such an impeachment resolution must be considered within two legislative days unless offered by the majority or minority leaders.

Rather than enduring the reading of another lengthy impeachment measure on the same day as the Trump resolution, the Speaker postponed its consideration to allow for other business to be conducted before the Thursday deadline for the Massie resolution’s consideration. That deadline prompted the Speaker to pull the switch on the rest of the week’s business late Wednesday. The House adjourned Thursday morning two minutes after convening.

The Hegseth impeachment resolution would likely have been tabled regardless of when it was considered. But the cumulative effect of so many negative attacks on the president’s policies and personnel was not the kind of positive message the Republicans wanted to bring home to their voters.

House Democrats were quick to pounce on the hasty Republican retreat, convening a press conference Thursday morning to charge Republicans with absenteeism and presiding over a “do-nothing Congress” at a time when Americans are facing higher gas and grocery prices and the president is waging an unpopular war with Iran. To back-up their do-nothing claims, Democrats cited 63 cancelled voting days in this Congress, plus three government shutdowns totaling a record-setting 100 days. Republicans countered that they have already had a productive two years, pointing especially to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of tax cuts and a crack-down on illegal immigration.

Yet, the do-nothing Congress charge cuts two ways. Most polls show public disapproval of Congress assigns blame for policy failures to both political parties. And, it is difficult for a minority party to convert its professed governing policy ambitions into convincing practical solutions when the party seems stuck in a cloud of diaphanous aspirations.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran, culminating as chief of staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial,” and “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays .”

articles.title: Susan Collins defies blue-state headwinds in crucial Senate battle as new poll reveals striking split
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Susan Collins leads Democrat Troy Jackson 49%-46% in a new Maine Senate poll, but her edge falls within the margin of error.
articles.body: A new poll indicates longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins is ahead of her Democratic challenger in a crucial Senate showdown in blue-leaning Maine. Collins, who is running for a sixth six-year term in the Senate, stands at 49% support among likely voters, with former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee, at 46%, with 5% undecided in the New York Times/Siena poll. Collins' three-point edge is within the survey's margin of error. Democrats are heavily targeting Collins as they work to flip the seat, which is key to their efforts to win back the Senate majority from the Republicans in the midterm elections. The survey, which was conducted Sept. 15–22, is one of the first to indicate Collins ahead of Jackson since he replaced former Senate nominee Graham Platner in late July. SIX FORCES THAT COULD HELP REPUBLICANS DEFY HISTORY IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Platner, a combat veteran and oyster farmer, won the June Democratic Senate primary in a landslide. But a month later he dropped out following an explosive report containing an allegation of rape from a woman he previously dated. Platner denied the report but stepped aside. Collins slightly trailed Platner in most polling at the time he ended his campaign. Jackson, who campaigned alongside Platner earlier this year as he unsuccessfully ran for governor, won a special nominating convention to fill the party's vacant Senate nomination. The poll release came as Collins pushed back against a report by ProPublica that the FBI sought to launch a pay-to-play investigation examining Collins and others. The investigation was later dropped and no one working for Collins was charged. Collins ripped the report as "offensive" and a "partisan hit job" orchestrated by Democrats. Jackson took to social media to claim that "Susan Collins is blatantly corrupt." Collins' advantage over Jackson in the new survey comes even as 55% of those questioned said they prefer Democrats to control the Senate next year, with 43% saying they'd like the GOP to retain the majority. COLLINS TEARS INTO NEW REPORT ALLEDGING PAY-TO PLAY SCHEME Likely boosting Collins are her favorable ratings, which are in positive territory, at 51%-48%. Meanwhile, Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and a one-time conservative Republican who became a Democrat over two decades ago and who is now running on a progressive platform, is underwater with 41% of those questioned viewing him favorably and 49% holding an unfavorable view. As he quickly became the frontrunner in the abbreviated race to replace Platner, Jackson faced a slew of media reports over his alleged temper and workplace conduct, as well as reported claims of mortgage improprieties and other potential liabilities, including his past strict anti-abortion stance. In August, a resurfaced 1988 police record which detailed accusations that Jackson assaulted a man and pushed his longtime partner during a late-night confrontation in Fort Kent, Maine, grabbed headlines. Jackson, in a statement, said, "I took responsibility for it then, and I take responsibility for it now. But let me be clear: I have never been violent with my partner Lana, or any other woman." WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM ELECTION POLLING Lana Pelletier, who, according to records, is Jackson's second cousin, shares two adult children with him. Collins, the only GOP senator seeking re-election in a state President Donald Trump lost in the 2024 election, is facing a rough political climate, amid Trump's underwater approval ratings, persistent inflation, soaring fuel prices and what polls indicate is an unpopular war with Iran. The senator, known as a moderate Republican who at times has voted against Trump, this summer received bipartisan praise after reaching a milestone by casting her 10,000th consecutive Senate vote. But Democrats are taking aim at Collins over her comments that she didn't regret her 2018 vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, despite his crucial vote four years later to overturn the landmark Roe v. Wade abortion ruling. And following the fatal shooting in Maine this summer involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, Democrats heavily criticized the Senate Appropriations Committee chair for her support for ICE funding. But Collins has broken with Trump numerous times in recent months, criticizing his tariff war with neighboring Canada and voting against Attorney General Todd Blanche's confirmation. The senator has a history of surviving Democratic efforts to unseat her. Six years ago, she trailed Democratic challenger Sara Gideon, the then-Maine House speaker, but the senator ended up winning re-election by nearly nine points while former President Joe Biden carried the state by a similar margin. Fox News Digital reached out to both the Collins and Jackson campaigns for comment on the new survey, but didn't receive a response at the time this story was published. In neighboring New Hampshire, the survey indicates Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas with a 50%-45% advantage over former Republican Sen. John E. Sununu, in the race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. Meanwhile, in Michigan, the poll indicates Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed ahead of former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers 49%-44% in the showdown to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. articles.title: Democrats sue Trump administration over threats to deploy federal agents to polls
articles.summary: Democratic Party leadership and campaign organizations sued the Trump administration Wednesday over alleged threats to unlawfully deploy armed federal agents to polling sites during the midterm elections. The lawsuit, which was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, accuses Trump administration law enforcement and immigration officials of demonstrating “by word and…
articles.body:
Democratic Party leadership and campaign organizations sued the Trump administration Wednesday over alleged threats to unlawfully deploy armed federal agents to polling sites during the midterm elections.

The lawsuit, which was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, accuses Trump administration law enforcement and immigration officials of demonstrating “by word and deed that they have established a policy of permitting their armed officers to appear at active polling sites.”

The plaintiffs in the case include Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y) as well as the Democratic campaign committees for both chambers of Congress and the Democratic Governors Association.

The Trump administration has stated that it does not have formal plans to send federal agents to the polls this November but has not ruled the possibility out.

But in February, President Trump’s call to “ nationalize the voting ” raised alarm from Democrats.

Attorneys for the plaintiffs cited Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s comments during a Sept. 1 press conference, in which the secretary said “the only reason” federal agents would be at a polling place is to respond to a threat or serve a warrant.

“DHS’s most recent statements confirm the existence of an agency policy that authorizes sending ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] officers to polling locations, so long as the agency either identifies a supposed ‘threat,’ is seeking to serve a warrant, or is engaged in routine immigration enforcement activities,” the attorneys wrote in their filing.

Additionally, attorneys for the Democratic plaintiffs pointed to FBI Director Kash Patel’s testimony to the Senate Judiciary Committee last week, in which Democrats on the panel pushed the director to commit to not sending FBI agents to the polls this November.

In response to a question from Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Patel said the agency would “follow the law.”

“If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation of law, we will,” he said. “Otherwise, we won’t.”

The Democrats pointed to examples of federal agents entering polling places during primary and runoff elections this midterm cycle.

In one instance cited in the filing from June, several ICE officers confronted an election worker at a polling location in Syracuse, N.Y., about her online criticism of the federal agency.

The Hill has reached out to the Justice Department, the White House and the Department of Homeland Security for comment.
