articles.title: The invisible threat to America’s classified intelligence
articles.summary: Without continuous monitoring for wireless devices, unauthorized devices could be transmitting classified information from inside, completely undetected.
articles.body:
“Someone in here has earbuds. Get them out now!”

That should be the immediate response when any wireless device is detected in a facility that is meant to be free of unauthorized electronics so that classified matters can be discussed without the risk of prying foreign adversaries. Unfortunately, most of these facilities aren’t consistently monitored for wireless intrusions, and breaches — intentional or otherwise — often go undetected.

Every day, phones, earbuds, smartwatches, fitness trackers, smart glasses, Bluetooth-enabled trackers (like AirTags) and other devices, each able to record and transmit, are brought into Sensitive Compartmented Information Facilities (known as “SCIFs”) and Special Access Program Facilities where America’s secrets are held and discussed.

These facilities are built to keep adversaries out of the nation’s most sensitive conversations, with guards, guns and gates. But without continuous monitoring for wireless devices, unauthorized devices could be transmitting classified information from inside, completely undetected.

Nearly every modern electronic device emits radio frequency signals to communicate across Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular and other protocols, often without deliberate user action. Glasses can now record and earbuds can instantly translate. And they can all transmit in real time to anyone outside these rooms bypassing guards, guns and gates. A single unauthorized device inside a secure facility can become a highway for sensitive information to be captured, transmitted or exposed.

Across the U.S. government, military and intelligence community, officials operate tens of thousands of secure facilities to discuss classified matters that can range from plans for the next-generation fighter jet or naval ship to intelligence about Iran’s nuclear capabilities or Russia’s war plans. The vast majority are not monitored for wireless devices.

All secure facilities are built to the same standards, whether it’s the walls, doors or alarms. The absence of continuous monitoring across our most sensitive facilities despite a 2023 order and 2024 deadline set by the secretary of Defense is a vulnerability that the government is aware of — and one that adversaries are actively exploiting.

This is not hypothetical. In March 2025, Army Sergeant Jian Zhao was indicted for conspiring to obtain and transmit national defense information to individuals in China, along with bribery and theft of government property. Prosecutors say he photographed classified documents at his desk at Joint Base Lewis-McChord with a smartphone, and then negotiated their sale for thousands of dollars. Surveillance images in the court file show him doing it, phone in hand, while he was in contact with his buyer. He also sold 20 classified hard drives and a stolen encryption-capable computer.

The same year, a U.S. State Department employee with a top-secret clearance was convicted of using an iPhone to photograph classified documents off his computer monitor and transmit them to people he believed were Chinese intelligence after receiving the phone, and $10,000, six months earlier.

And these are just a couple of the public cases and details we know about. The risk is growing faster than the response, as wireless devices become increasingly vulnerable to hacks. Nearly 1,000 new wireless vulnerabilities were disclosed in 2025 alone , according to an analysis of National Vulnerability Database records.

Detecting wireless devices isn’t new. While the U.S. has had systems for indoor settings for more than a decade, they are not up to the task of detecting the latest technologies, whether it’s Bluetooth or smart glasses that can record surreptitiously. Modern threats require modern protection that provides real-time visibility, allowing for immediate removal before an unauthorized disclosure has occurred.

In the last five years, the government and commercial enterprises have begun using a new generation of “ Wireless Intrusion Detection Systems ” that have been engineered for accuracy, advanced protocols and identification and detection of active transmissions. These modern indoor systems are used by security teams without special radiofrequency training.

So, while a 2023 Pentagon requirement mandating the installation of such systems in all department SCIFs and Special Access Program Facilities may have appeared prohibitively expensive a decade ago, they are now within reach of military budgets. Monitoring costs an order of magnitude less than new construction or retrofitting spaces.

Continuous wireless monitoring systems can monitor Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular and Internet of things spectrums in real time, and detect and locate unauthorized devices without requiring agencies to physically reconstruct every secure facility. These systems are deployed today in a small fraction of secure facilities and across corporate offices and AI data centers, and are producing significant results.

Though this has been a requirement since 2023, it still needs to be funded. The Department of Defense must define the continuous wireless detection requirement and submit the requisite funding request. Congress can then include this requirement in the forthcoming National Defense Authorization Act and appropriations bills.

America’s adversaries are patient and thorough. They are exploiting every available gap, including the invisible wireless environment. If we’re not careful, the next intelligence leak may come through a device someone “forgot” was in their pocket, on their wrist or authorized and in their ear.

Vice Adm. Jeffrey Trussler (Ret.) is former director of naval intelligence and deputy chief of naval operations for information warfare. David M. Taylor is a senior U.S. government official who performed the duties of the undersecretary and deputy undersecretary of Defense for intelligence and security.

articles.title: Dem Senate hopeful rocked by explosive ex-aide claims as campaign cites ‘hardest period of her life’
articles.summary: Mary Peltola says her alleged outbursts came amid grief after losing her mother and husband months apart, pushing back on the New York Times report.
articles.body: Former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska, is facing allegations from former aides that she erupted in anger, used offensive slurs, sent profane text messages and once shoved a staffer — claims her campaign disputes while denying that they reflect a broader pattern of abusive behavior. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that former Peltola aides alleged she was quick to anger, used anti-gay slurs and a slur targeting the mentally handicapped, sent edgy text messages and, in one case, shoved an employee. Though Peltola’s campaign disputed several of the allegations, her spokesman said some of her behavior came during a period of extreme grief after the deaths of her mother and husband in 2023. "Mary suddenly and tragically lost both her mother and her husband in the span of a few months in 2023. At the time of their passing, Mary was parenting kids through their own grief, serving full-time in the U.S. House of Representatives thousands of miles from home, and running a competitive re-election campaign – all while shouldering the enormous burden of grief," a spokesman for her campaign told the media in response to the report. FETTERMAN LEANS ON UNLIKELY GOP ALLY AS DEMS SHARPEN THEIR KNIVES OVER EXPLOSIVE REPORT "Like any person who has gone through multiple personal tragedies in the span of a few months, Mary sometimes struggled to deal with her grief. But she treats her staff with respect and care, and she maintains close positive relationships with her staff spanning her nearly 30 years in public service," the spokesman continued. "Exaggerating and outright lying about moments from the hardest period of her life, and falsely presenting them as a pattern of behavior, is wrong." Peltola avoided reporters’ questions about the allegations after a Wednesday town hall, leaving without responding, Alaska News Source reported. While much of the behavior described in the New York Times article, such as Peltola’s alleged use of slurs and the shove, occurred during the aftermath of her personal tragedies, other incidents purportedly happened more recently. The atmosphere in Peltola’s congressional office allegedly drove aides to tears and prompted discussions about quitting, with some saying the stress caused them to lose weight or seek therapy, according to the New York Times. The outlet separately described anxiety and exhaustion among staff on her 2026 Senate campaign. BAD BOSSES ON CAPITOL HILL COULD FACE RECKONING UNDER NEW ANONYMOUS STAFFER REVIEW PLATFORM Some commentators from across the political spectrum defended Peltola or questioned the significance of some of the allegations. "I think most reasonably well-adjusted people would read this and feel pretty sympathetic toward Peltola rather than her annoying staffers," left-of-center pollster Nate Silver said of the reporting. A Democratic communications staffer noted that getting yelled at by your boss is relatively normal on the Hill. "Call me crazy, but I do not think it's very objectionable for Mary Peltola, who commutes from Alaska to Washington DC, to ask a staffer to feed her pet," Robby Soave, who writes for a libertarian magazine, said. Not everyone took the Senate hopeful’s side, however. "Mary Peltola has a problem with violence and aggression, and she doesn't deserve to be dog-catcher let alone a U.S. Senator. Mary should apologize for her unhinged behavior," Republican National Committee spokesman Nick Poche said of the reporting. "I thought Peltola was boring and useless until I read this," former Rep. Matt Gaetz wrote on X. "Was this leaked to help Peltola with Alaskan men?" Staffers complained to the New York Times about having to feed live crickets to Peltola's pet chameleon, Meatball. Some of the staffers who complained about the working conditions in Peltola’s congressional office returned to work for her Senate campaign. DEM SENATE HOPEFUL VOWS TO UNLEASH ALASKA OIL — BUT HER RECORD TELLS A DIFFERENT STORY Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan are the leading contenders in Alaska’s four-candidate general election for U.S. Senate, which will likely be one of the closest Senate elections of this cycle. Though traditionally a red state, shifting voter preferences combined with Peltola’s unique crossover appeal have put Alaska in play for the Democrats. articles.title: Carville: Trump ‘wants to destroy’ Washington, DC
articles.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville said Wednesday that President Trump’s attempts to reshape and rename multiple landmarks throughout and just outside Washington, D.C., as well as create new ones, point to his “particular hatred” for the nation’s capital. Carville discussed on his podcast “Politics War Room” the MS NOW report that Trump pushed to have his…
articles.body:
Democratic strategist James Carville said Wednesday that President Trump’s attempts to reshape and rename multiple landmarks throughout and just outside Washington, D.C., as well as create new ones, point to his “particular hatred” for the nation’s capital.

Carville discussed on his podcast “ Politics War Room ” the MS NOW report that Trump pushed to have his name added in some way to Ford’s Theatre , the historic site where Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth assassinated former President Abraham Lincoln in 1865.

The report follows the repeated efforts of the Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board to add his name to that performing arts center.

“Trump has a particular hatred for Washington, D.C.,” Carville said. “Why do you think he is trying to defile everything he can, from the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery to the Reflecting Pool to the White House to every gauche thing he could think of?”

He later added that Trump “wants to destroy Washington, and I lived there for a long time … It’s a beautiful city.” The reported suggestion of Trump adding his name to Ford’s Theatre was “just one more thing he” could do.

The onetime campaign strategist to former President Clinton said he was reminded of remarks made to him years ago by former Sen. Russell Long (D-La.).

“He said, you know, ‘It looks like a major world capital,’ when you go to Washington and the buildings, and it screams republican, small ‘R’ republican,” Carville continued. “We’re not an empire, we don’t do that. I think Trump hates all of that. I think he hates what Washington is, what Washington stands for.”

More than 90 percent of D.C. residents voted against Trump in the 2024 election.

Carville accused Trump of not liking the city’s architecture and the “inherent modesty that comes with being part of a Constitution that was written and went into effect in 1789.” He added that people who can afford it should visit the city “to find out it’s one f‑‑‑ing impressive place.”

Trump dismissed MS NOW’s reporting Wednesday as “a ridiculous lie,” “FAKE NEWS” and “just another one of their never-ending, malicious falsehoods to try to discredit and demean.”

The report stated that former and current White House officials said there were discussions to rename the landmark, with some of the president’s close allies pitching his name as a contender in an effort to please him.

Ford’s Theatre and the Petersen House across the street, where Lincoln died the morning after he was shot, were collectively designated by the National Park Service as a National Historic Site.

The Trump administration has attempted to change Washington’s landmarks with several proposed, in-development or completed projects, including a triumphal arch between Washington and Arlington National Cemetery, as well as changes to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and the Kennedy Center.

Changes made to the Kennedy Center, including the president’s hand-picked board voting to add his name to the building, have resulted in an ongoing legal dispute over Trump’s name on the building and the administration’s insistence that the performing arts center is in dire need of renovations.

articles.title: Journalists for CNN, MS Now, Politico allowed back in White House following Trump ban
articles.summary: Journalists for CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back onto White House grounds Thursday, hours after a judge ruled in the outlets’ favor following President Trump’s decision to ban the media organizations from the building last week. The networks reported on air that their reporters and photographers were initially denied access early Thursday but…
articles.body:
Journalists for CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back onto White House grounds Thursday, hours after a judge ruled in the outlets’ favor following President Trump’s decision to ban the media organizations from the building last week.

The networks reported on air that their reporters and photographers were initially denied access early Thursday but were allowed into the building after attorneys for the companies petitioned a judge urging him compel the White House to respond to their requests for re-entry.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the administration to restore access “immediately” overnight, after an emergency hearing on Wednesday. MS Now, CNN and Politico argued their due process and First Amendment rights were violated by Trump’s ban .

“Defendants do not dispute that Plaintiffs did not receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before their hard passes were revoked,” Kelly, a Trump appointee, wrote as part of his opinion.

After the reporters were still blocked earlier Thursday, attorney Theodore Boutrous — who represented the outlets — wrote to Kelly saying “time is of the essence.”

“CNN is scheduled to be the television pool this evening for President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House,” he said at the time, arguing the Trump administration “already repeatedly violated the Court’s Order.”

The president barred the outlets from the White House last week for what he called their publishing of “fake news,” while the Department of Justice argued the reporting put national security at risk.

The move was widely condemned by press freedom groups and political observers, who predicted Kelly would rule in the outlet’s favor.

Neither the White House nor President Trump have provided comment on the judge’s late-night ruling.

In a filing with the court on Thursday, the director of press operations at the White House wrote his office was notified at 7:10 a.m. to restore the outlet’s access.

The office began that process at 7:25 a.m., the White House said, and U.S. Secret Service indicated badges were back on at 9:07 a.m.

The White House press team turned confiscated badges over to the Secret Service at 9:55 a.m., according to the filing, and they were then distributed to impacted reporters just after noon on Thursday.

Kelly’s late night ruling is valid for 14 days, and it was unclear as of Thursday if the Trump administration was planning an appeal.

Trump in a social media post earlier this week cast doubt on his chances of defeating the news outlets’ suit, writing “almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”

articles.title: US allies need to shoot down Russian aircraft testing NATO boundaries, Czech president warns
articles.summary: Czech President Petr Pavel warned NATO may need to shoot down Russian aircraft or drones deliberately violating allied airspace to avoid weakness.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Czech President Petr Pavel insists that NATO needs to outright demonstrate its willingness to respond to Russian aggression or else Moscow will continue to push the alliance and its European boundaries. "There might be the time when we will have to shoot down some of these planes or unmanned vehicles that are testing our readiness," Pavel, a retired general and former chair of NATO's Military Committee, predicted in a conversation with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York City this week. Pavel said alliance members understandably want to avoid escalation, but risk sending the wrong signal as he warned Moscow views restraint as weakness and is testing allied defenses with its continued aggression. "What I am afraid of is that they see a lack of will on our side to take decisive action," Pavel said. "Within Russian perceptions it demonstrates weakness. And they respect power." The warning followed fresh incidents along NATO’s eastern flank, where a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter crossed from Kaliningrad into Polish airspace Wednesday, prompting Poland to scramble fighter jets. Romania scrambled F-16s Thursday after another unidentified aerial target crossed its border from Ukraine. Denmark’s military intelligence service also warned Thursday that Russia is likely to intensify hybrid attacks against NATO in the coming months and assessed a "low but growing" risk of a limited Russian military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia. ROMANIAN F-16 SHOOTS DOWN DRONE AFTER AIRSPACE BREACH, MARKING FIRST FOR NATO ALLY Pavel said in a speech before the U.N. General Assembly Wednesday that Russia's "aggressive posture poses a direct threat to European security" and warned that the risk is growing. He told Fox News Digital that the pattern of recent escalation was familiar from his years at NATO, recalling Russian aircraft testing U.S. pilots over Syria and repeatedly violating Turkish airspace before Turkey shot down a Russian warplane in 2015. "They are, on one hand, provoking. On the other, testing what will our reaction be," Pavel detailed. NATO already has procedures for accidental airspace violations, Pavel said, including warning aircraft and attempting to establish contact. But he drew a distinction between mistakes and aircraft that deliberately enter allied airspace and refuse to respond. "If it is deliberate and the violator doesn’t respond to our measures, then we will have to act, because otherwise Russia simply would push further on," the Czech president added. RUSSIA'S NEIGHBOR REVEALS PERSONAL APPEALS TO TRUMP AS US WEIGHS NATO TROOP PULLBACK IN EUROPE The comments come amid recent drone incursions involving NATO members along the alliance’s eastern flank, including incidents in Poland, Romania and Lithuania. Pavel was similarly skeptical that President Vladimir Putin is serious about talks to end the war in Ukraine, saying he has seen no significant Russian effort to negotiate. He argued that while Moscow publicly expresses willingness to hold talks, the conditions it has attached would effectively strip Ukraine of sovereignty. He said a genuine negotiating process would require Russia to agree to a ceasefire first and then enter talks without preconditions. RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS The Czech president also warned that the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed another vulnerability across the NATO alliance: depleted weapons stockpiles and defense-production systems struggling to keep pace with demand. "With the amount of ammunition, especially intelligent ammunition, consumed over a short period of time, we all understand on both sides of the Atlantic how short we are when it comes to stocks of these kinds of equipment," Pavel said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He said the lesson for both Europe and the United States is to accelerate weapons production and overhaul procurement systems he described as "extremely long and rigid." Pavel’s warning underscores a broader challenge facing NATO as it weighs how forcefully to respond to Russian activity without triggering a wider confrontation, while simultaneously replenishing the military stockpiles needed to sustain deterrence over the longer term.

Programming note : We’re Claire Leibowitz and Abigail Walker, filling in for Cate today. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cleibowitz@thehill.com or awalker@thehill.com.

The White House must immediately restore press access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, a federal judge ruled early Thursday.

After being denied entry this morning, CNN and MS NOW are saying their reporters have regained White House access mid-morning.

ABC is the assigned TV pooler today. But Jeremy Barr of the Guardian had this update in the morning: “I am told they are in a bit of a stand-off with the White House staff and are refusing to go into any events until they have proof CNN is on campus.”

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the White House to lift the ban following an emergency hearing Wednesday. In his ruling, Kelly cited a lack of due process regarding the president’s ban.

“Defendants do not dispute that Plaintiffs did not receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before their hard passes were revoked,” the federal judge, a Trump appointee, wrote.

What now? CNN, MS NOW, Politico asked Kelly this morning for an immediate hearing over White House noncompliance with his order, which is meant to last for two weeks.

The judge gave the Department of Justice until 12:30 this afternoon to reply.

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived yesterday for an anticipated state visit, with talks getting underway this afternoon on a range of topics.

He announced on Thursday that China will gift two pandas to the U.S. and is inviting 100,000 American students to study in China. The pandas will head to Zoo Atlanta in Atlanta, Ga.

“The hope of China-U.S. relationship lies in our people, and its future lies with the young,” he said.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday that the U.S. and China will extend their trade agreement until January, taking some of the urgency out of Trump-Xi talks on that issue.

AI on the menu: Trump and Xi are also expected to discuss ways the two nations can team up to manage artificial intelligence , which has stirred fear in recent months among lawmakers and industry executives.

In a Thursday speech, Xi said the U.S. and China have obligations to monitor AI’s advancements.

“We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” Xi said.

“Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is,” the American president wrote earlier on Thursday on Truth Social, referring to his new name for AI. “That is China’s position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ!”

And the literal menu? Trump will host Xi for a state dinner at the White House on Thursday.

“The menu showcases American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence, bringing the culinary traditions of both nations together,” first lady Melania Trump ’s office said.

As is typical for formal gatherings like tonight’s, symbolism plays a heavy had.

The Hill’s Tara Suter notes : “The first lady’s office selected Schramsberg Blanc De Noir as the dinner’s wine accompaniment, which it says is a reference to the 1972 ‘Toast to Peace’ between former President Nixon and former Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai in Beijing.”

An Emerson College Polling survey released Thursday found Democrats led Republicans on a generic congressional ballot at 53 percent and 42 percent, respectively.

“While the generic ballot test doesn’t capture nuances of individual races, it’s an important metric to gauge the magnitude of a potential Democratic wave,” Spencer Kimball , executive director of Emerson College Polling, explained in a Thursday press release.

But RNC Chair Joe Gruters on Wednesday night said he expects his party to maintain its majorities in Congress. He told Blake Burman on NewsNation’s “The Hill” that he predicts the GOP will clinch 220 seats in the House and 53 in the Senate.

“We have our secret weapon and president, Donald J. Trump, and I say that because we’re going to barnstorm the country,” Gruters said. “We’re going to do lots of rallies … and we’re going to deliver for the American people.”

Meanwhile, Trump’s disapproval rating looks…high: It hit its highest mark yet — 58 percent — amid rising energy costs and economic woes, per an Emerson College poll.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) leads Democrat Troy Jackson by 3 points in her bid for a sixth term, a New York Times/Siena University survey found.

The incumbent’s edge was within the roughly 5-point margin of error, while another 5 percent of the 619 respondents were undecided.

It’s been a roller-coaster week for Collins. A bombshell ProPublica report on Tuesday said that the FBI was investigating an alleged pay-to-play scheme between the senator’s office, a pro-Collins super PAC and defense contractor Navatek, before the probe was dropped when Trump returned to office.

She and her team have denied the claims, with Collins calling the report “a partisan hit job.” ProPublica responded in a follow-up piece , saying “some of her claims aren’t true.”

Collins also faces a test of her pro-choice bona fides with a confirmation hearing for anti-abortion Dr. Heidi Overton, Trump’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration.

The senator has kept her concerns quiet, The Hill’s Nathaniel Weixel reports . Collins told him that she raised the issue of abortion in a private meeting with the doctor.

“That’s one issue, but another is vaccines and third is the slow pace that FDA approves treatments and medications in cases where there are rare diseases for which there are no medications currently on the market,” Collins said.

Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa are leading GOP opponents Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott , a Marist Poll Texas survey finds .

Former President Barack Obama said in his newly launched literary-focused podcast that the federal government is “so much less corrupt” today than it was in the past.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) on Wednesday accused Iran’s leaders of being “part of a colony of reptiles,” and grouped them with other U.S. adversaries , including China, North Korea and Russia.

articles.summary: Democrats appear to be gaining ground with young men, a key voting bloc for the GOP’s success last election cycle, ahead of the midterms, according to a new survey released on Thursday. articles.body:
Democrats appear to be gaining ground with young men, a key voting bloc for the GOP’s success last election cycle, ahead of the midterms, according to a new survey released on Thursday.

The Cygnal poll found that likely male voters between the ages of 18 and 30 were more likely to support a Democrat over a Republican on a generic ballot this November.

Around 52 percent of survey respondents selected the Democratic candidate option, while about 42 percent said they would elect a Republican candidate. Five percent said they were unsure.

Politico was the first to report on the survey’s results.

Exit polling from the 2024 election showed Republicans with a slight advantage among this voting demographic, with just over half of men between the ages of 18 and 29 supporting President Trump over Vice President Kamala Harris in that year’s presidential race.

Former President Joe Biden won a similar share of male voters in this age group in the 2020 presidential race, and this new poll could be an indication that young American men are moving back in the favor of Democrats this November.

Over 55 percent of the young men surveyed in the Cygnal poll said they held an unfavorable view of Trump and around 48 percent had a negative view of the Republican Party overall. The Democratic Party fared slightly better, but still had a net-negative favorability rating among these voters.

The survey also asked respondents about which policy objectives would make the “biggest difference” in their lives. Thirty-eight percent indicated that lowering grocery and everyday costs would make the largest impact, while nearly 32 percent selected more affordable housing options.

The Cygnal poll was conducted among 800 registered male voters between the ages of 18 and 30 from Sept. 15-18 with a margin of error of approximately 3.46 percentage points.

articles.title: Missouri election map fight races back toward Supreme Court after 1.2M voters cast primary ballots
articles.summary: The Eighth Circuit ruled Missouri must use its 2025 congressional map for the general election, but the Supreme Court could intervene before Sept. 28.
articles.body: Missouri’s congressional map fight is hurtling toward another potential Supreme Court showdown, with courts at odds over which districts should govern the November election after more than 1.2 million Missourians voted in the August primary under a different map. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit ruled Monday that Missouri must use its 2025 congressional map in November, finding that switching to the state’s 2022 districts after the primary would violate the U.S. Constitution. But the appeals court paused its order until Sept. 28, 2026, opening a narrow window for another visit to the U.S. Supreme Court. Abhishek Kambli, a partner at Holtzman Vogel and former deputy associate attorney general at the Justice Department, told Fox News Digital the Supreme Court’s previous intervention does not necessarily signal how the justices will handle the latest ruling. "It’s unpredictable how they’ll rule, mostly because we didn’t get their reasoning in the last order," Kambli said. "So, we don’t know the precise reason why they decided to stay at that time." ELECTION CHAOS IN THIS RED STATE JUST GOT EVEN STRANGER FOR REPUBLICANS AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING The Supreme Court previously stayed a federal district court's temporary restraining order requiring Missouri to use the 2025 map. The Eighth Circuit has now directed the lower court to enter a permanent injunction requiring the newer districts, putting the dispute in a different procedural posture. "So unless the Supreme Court steps in again, the state will be required to use the seven-one map for this election," Kambli said. Missouri held its Aug. 4, 2026, primary under the 2025 map. Roughly a month later, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled that voters could challenge the map through a referendum, leaving the 2022 districts in place for the November election. Kambli said switching congressional maps between the primary and general election raises serious constitutional concerns. "You would have had a large number of Missourians who would have been disenfranchised because they voted for one set of candidates in the primary and will be voting for another set in the general," Kambli said. MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP "And what's even more concerning is sometimes those candidates are unopposed so that they miss their only chance to vote as a result of what the Missouri Supreme Court did here," Kambli continued. "So that's what's really at issue — is whether everyone gets an equal voice in a situation where the primary election is integral to the electoral system of the state." But Yale law professor Akhil Amar and University of California, Davis, law professor Vikram Amar have argued the opposite. After the Supreme Court’s earlier stay, Vikram wrote on SCOTUSblog that using the 2025 map in November would not protect anyone’s right to vote if those lines were never legally in effect. Akhil agreed with his analysis. "HB1’s district lines lack the force of law, full stop," Vikram wrote. "These lines cannot be used wrongly in November just because they were previously used wrongly in the primary. Two wrongs do not make (or vindicate) a right (to vote)." Meanwhile, Kambli placed much of the blame for the eleventh-hour legal scramble over which map to use on the Missouri Supreme Court, arguing the turmoil was "entirely preventable." VIRGINIA GOP, DEMS BATTLE IT OUT OVER REDISTRICTING BEFORE STATE SUPREME COURT Kambli argued that the Missouri Supreme Court could have resolved the map dispute earlier, noting that the issue remained unsettled even after the candidate filing deadline passed. Alicia Bannon, senior director of the Judiciary Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, pointed instead to delays by Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins as a key reason the dispute dragged on. Opponents of the 2025 map submitted more than 300,000 signatures in December 2025, but Hoskins did not formally reject the referendum petition until Aug. 4, the day of the primary. "Time passed. And passed further," Bannon wrote for State Court Report. "As early as December 2025, Hoskins asserted in separate federal litigation that a referendum on redistricting was not authorized by the state constitution. But he held off on issuing a certificate on that basis — which would have triggered judicial review — instead going through a lengthy process of verifying petition signatures." Bannon wrote that the Missouri Supreme Court’s criticism of Hoskins’ delays stood out, particularly the court’s rejection of his argument that it had waited too long to intervene. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The Missouri Supreme Court ultimately ruled that the referendum could proceed and faulted Hoskins for the delay, saying he had "created the confusion, expense, and practical difficulties of which he complains." Kambli argued the Purcell principle, under which federal courts generally avoid changing election rules close to Election Day because of the potential for disruption, weighs in favor of keeping the 2025 map because Missouri already used it for the primary. "The Eighth Circuit said that the Purcell principles support the injunction, not go against it," Kambli said. Bannon also warned that courts being too cautious can create its own problems. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It’s an approach that’s understandable in some circumstances but can also incentivize shenanigans to evade judicial review while harming voters’ rights," Bannon wrote. Bannon suggested earlier court action in Missouri could have helped avoid the last-minute dispute, including by moving the primary or setting a firm deadline for the referendum petition. But regardless of whether the Supreme Court decides to weigh in, the referendum will still be on the ballot. "If the Supreme Court does not stay the Eighth Circuit injunction, there's no doubt that the 7-1 map is what will be in effect for this election. There's still going to be a referendum on the ballot deciding that issue for future elections, but for this one, that's how it'll be decided," Kambli said.
